Pettle did file a report with local police — six officers, he says, took his statement and had him sign it. What strikes him most, looking back, is what they never asked for: the names of the men involved, which he had; the passport used, which he had; or a single phone number from the dozens who called him during the ordeal.



“This is the beginning of a dormant complaint,” Pettle writes. But his closing line is the one that lingers: despite everything, he says his real ambition is still “to come back and bring investment to your beautiful country” — if Liberia will have him.

World.title: After 35 Years, Liberia Reopens Embassy in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI, India — Liberia has officially reopened its Embassy in New Delhi after more than 35 years without a resident diplomatic mission in India, marking a major step in efforts to strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries.

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti is in New Delhi to formally inaugurate the Embassy on behalf of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Government and people of Liberia.

The Liberian Embassy in India was closed more than three decades ago amid geopolitical and other challenges facing the country. Successive administrations subsequently sought to restore a permanent diplomatic presence in India, recognizing the country’s growing importance as a partner in Asia.

The reopening culminates years of efforts spanning several administrations. The Government said President Boakai’s administration has built on earlier initiatives to complete the process and restore Liberia’s resident diplomatic presence in New Delhi.

Speaking ahead of the inauguration, Minister Nyanti described the reopening as both a diplomatic milestone and an opportunity to deliver practical benefits to Liberians.

“After more than three decades, Liberia once again has a permanent diplomatic home in India,” Nyanti said. “This is a major milestone for our country and a testament to President Boakai’s commitment to strengthening Liberia’s global partnerships and ensuring that our diplomacy delivers tangible results for our people.”

She also acknowledged the efforts of successive administrations that worked toward reestablishing the mission.

The reopening is particularly significant given the growing number of Liberian students pursuing education and professional training in India, as well as Liberians traveling there for medical treatment.

The resident Embassy is expected to strengthen consular services and provide more direct assistance to Liberian citizens while creating opportunities for scholarships, education, healthcare and professional capacity building.

Beyond consular services, the Embassy is expected to serve as Liberia’s principal diplomatic and economic platform in India, with a focus on attracting investment, promoting trade and private-sector partnerships, and expanding cooperation in agriculture, technology, infrastructure and healthcare.

The mission will also support Liberia’s broader economic diplomacy and national development priorities by helping mobilize technical assistance and development partnerships.

India remains an important development and economic partner for Liberia, with bilateral cooperation spanning education, health, agriculture, technology, infrastructure, capacity building, trade and private-sector development.

The Government of Liberia expressed appreciation to India for its cooperation and support in facilitating the reopening of the Embassy and said the development marks a new chapter in Liberia–India relations.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Demands Independent Probe Into Cocaine Crisis
World.content:
Monrovia — As Liberia grapples with the fallout from its largest-ever cocaine seizures, renowned Liberian lawyer and politician Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has issued one of his strongest warnings yet, describing the country’s escalating narcotics problem as a national security emergency and cautioning that Liberia must not follow the path of Haiti, where criminal networks have severely weakened state authority.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

In a lengthy commentary, Gongloe called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to establish an independent Commission of Inquiry to investigate the cocaine seizures, trace the money behind the alleged trafficking network and determine whether individuals within Liberia’s security and political establishment helped facilitate the operation.

“Liberia must not become Haiti,” Gongloe declared, warning that the country could face a gradual erosion of state authority if corruption, organized crime and compromised security institutions are not confronted decisively.

Gongloe, a former standard-bearer of the Liberian People’s Party who contested the 2023 presidential election, said the scale of the cocaine seizures demonstrates that Liberia is confronting more than a conventional law-enforcement problem.

According to authorities, approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at more than US$19 million, were seized at Roberts International Airport in June. The country was subsequently rocked by the discovery of approximately 3,971 kilograms — nearly four metric tons — of cocaine, estimated to be worth about US$317 million, in the Duazon area.

Gongloe said the volume and value of the drugs point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.

“This is not the work of a few young people selling drugs on a street corner,” he said. “The sheer volume and value point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.”

He said investigators must determine who imported the drugs, who received and transported them, who provided protection, and whether anyone within the Liberian state facilitated the operation.

‘Follow the Money’

Central to Gongloe’s proposed response is a comprehensive financial investigation.

“The central principle must be simple: follow the money,” he said.

He argued that the investigation should extend beyond the cocaine itself to financial transactions, unexplained wealth, properties, businesses, bank accounts, communications, airport records, immigration records, shipping records and political relationships.

“Cocaine is the commodity. Money is the motive. Corruption is often the bridge between criminal money and legitimate institutions,” Gongloe said.

He stressed that allegations against individuals must not be treated as established facts and that anyone accused of wrongdoing must be afforded due process and presumed innocent until proven guilty.

But he said due process cannot become an excuse for government inaction.

“The rule of law does not mean that government should remain silent when credible allegations of criminal conduct reach into the highest levels of government,” he said. “The rule of law requires a fearless, impartial and professional investigation.”

Calls for Independent Commission

Gongloe acknowledged actions already taken by the Boakai administration, including reported suspensions, dismissals, arrests, charges and detentions involving individuals connected to the investigation.

He praised the administration for taking steps in the direction of accountability but said the measures remain insufficient given the magnitude of the crisis.

“Mr. President, this is not enough,” Gongloe said.

He urged President Boakai to establish a commission composed of experts in criminal investigation, narcotics trafficking, financial intelligence, forensic accounting, money laundering, organized crime, constitutional and criminal law, cybersecurity, border security and asset tracing.

The commission, he said, should have the authority to obtain documents and testimony, trace financial transactions and examine relevant communications and movements.

Its findings, he added, should be made public, subject only to legitimate national-security restrictions.

Warning About State Capture

Gongloe said Liberia should study Haiti’s experience as a warning of what could happen when criminal organizations become stronger than state institutions.

He argued that institutional collapse does not happen overnight, but through a gradual process in which corruption becomes normalized, criminal networks purchase protection, security institutions become compromised, and young people are recruited into criminal enterprises.

“A country does not wake up one morning and discover that gangs control its streets,” he said. “Institutional deterioration occurs gradually.”

He warned that Liberia must confront the warning signs before organized crime becomes entrenched.

“That is the road Liberia must refuse to travel,” he said.

Beyond Cocaine

Gongloe linked the cocaine crisis to what he described as deeper problems of governance, corruption, weak institutions, impunity and unexplained wealth.

He raised questions about several other national controversies, including the multimillion-dollar project in Foya, Lofa County, and allegations surrounding illegal mining activities along the Liberia-Guinea border.

Gongloe was careful to distinguish questions from accusations, emphasizing that he was not alleging that the Foya project was financed with drug money.

Instead, he argued that the government should provide complete transparency about the project’s financing, procurement and authorization.

“If the money is legitimate, transparency should establish that fact,” he said. “If the procurement was lawful, the records should establish it.”

He similarly called for investigations into allegations of illegal mining along the Makona River, saying illicit mineral extraction could become a corruption, revenue, border-security and national-security problem.

A Message to Boakai

Gongloe also invoked President Boakai’s 2023 campaign-era remark that he could “dance with the devil” if doing so would help him win the presidency.

He said he was not suggesting that Boakai had any agreement with drug traffickers or that the president’s statement was connected to the cocaine crisis. Instead, Gongloe used the remark as a broader warning about political compromises.

“Every compromise with corruption has a price. Every accommodation with criminality has a price,” he said.

He described the “devil” metaphorically as corruption, greed, impunity, political patronage and abuse of public office.

“The real devil in Liberia is not a supernatural being,” Gongloe said. “The real devil is corruption. The real devil is greed. The real devil is impunity.”

Youth at Risk

Gongloe said Liberia’s young population is particularly vulnerable to recruitment by international narcotics networks because of unemployment, poverty and limited economic opportunities.

He warned that drug traffickers have the financial resources to offer young people opportunities that legitimate employment cannot match.

“What happens when a young Liberian begins to believe that a drug dealer has more opportunities than a university graduate?” he asked.

He said Liberia’s response must therefore go beyond arrests and prosecutions to include education, employment, public health, youth development, criminal justice and border security.

“Arrests alone will not solve it,” he said. “We must destroy the economic ecosystem that makes narcotics profitable.”

‘No One Should Be Above the Law’

Gongloe urged the government to investigate anyone connected to the drug-trafficking network regardless of political affiliation, social status or proximity to power.

“If the evidence leads to a poor man, investigate him. If it leads to a police officer, investigate him. If it leads to a businessman, investigate him. If it leads to a minister, investigate him,” he said.

“If it leads to someone close to the President, investigate him.”

He emphasized that the objective should not be to target individuals but to establish the truth and protect the Republic.

“No one should be above the law,” he said. “Not because we want to destroy people, but because we want to save Liberia.”

‘The System Must Be Examined’

Gongloe said the eventual destruction of the seized cocaine should not mark the end of the investigation.

“The cocaine may be destroyed. The suspects may eventually be convicted or acquitted. But the system that allowed such an enormous criminal enterprise to operate in Liberia must be examined,” he said.

He called on the government to identify the facilitators, protectors and beneficiaries of the alleged trafficking network and ensure that prosecutions follow where evidence warrants.

He also urged Liberians to resist turning the crisis into another partisan political dispute.

“Do not ask first whether the matter involves the Unity Party, the CDC or the LPP,” he said. “Ask whether Liberia is safe.”

Gongloe said the crisis represents a test for the presidency, security institutions, courts, Legislature and political parties — but ultimately, a test for the Liberian nation.

“We survived civil war. We survived Ebola. We survived political instability. We must not now lose Liberia to organized crime,” he said.

His central demand to President Boakai was repeated throughout the commentary: establish an independent inquiry, follow the money, follow the evidence, and ensure that justice reaches everyone implicated.

“Liberia deserves the truth,” Gongloe said.

“The cocaine may be seized. The cocaine may be destroyed. But the lesson must not be destroyed with it.”

He concluded with a stark warning: “If we do not control the criminals, the criminals may eventually control us. If we do not defeat corruption, corruption may eventually defeat the Republic.”

“Liberia must answer those questions, and Liberia must answer them now.”

World.title: Liberia: Why Prophetkey’s Six-Month Sentence Has Not Yet Guaranteed His Freedom
World.content:
MONROVIA — For months, the date August 13 had been viewed by supporters of Justin Oldpa Yeazehn, widely known as “Prophet Key,” as the day the controversial social media commentator would finally leave the Monrovia Central Prison.

By Willie N. Tokpah & Selma Lomax

The date represented the end of a six-month chapter that began with one of the most consequential contempt proceedings involving a Liberian social media personality. Yet, as the anticipated release date arrived, the expectation of freedom collided with a more complicated legal reality.

Prophet Key’s case has entered a stage in which the expiration of his custodial sentence is only one part of the equation. The Supreme Court of Liberia attached additional obligations to its February 13, 2026 decision, and the reported uncertainty surrounding compliance with those obligations has now placed his release in doubt.

What was expected to be a final day behind bars has instead become another chapter in a legal saga that has moved from social media broadcasts to the courtroom, from courtroom proceedings to imprisonment, and now from imprisonment to a debate over what must happen before the prison gates can finally open.

When the Calendar Was Supposed to End the Story

For Prophet Key’s supporters, the six-month sentence appeared straightforward. He was sentenced to 180 days at the Monrovia Central Prison after the Supreme Court found him guilty of criminal contempt. Once the period had elapsed, the natural expectation was that he would be released.

But the February ruling did more than impose a custodial sentence. The Supreme Court ordered Prophet Key to publish an apology to the judiciary and Liberian women in three local newspapers for five consecutive days. He was also required to execute a behavior bond in which he would commit himself to refraining from the conduct that resulted in his conviction.

That distinction has become central to the uncertainty surrounding his release. The issue is not simply whether Prophet Key has physically spent six months in prison. The question is whether the conditions accompanying the Court’s order have been fulfilled in a manner acceptable to the institution that imposed them.

That is why the approach of August 13 did not necessarily bring an automatic conclusion to the case.

The Case Behind the Bars

Prophet Key’s imprisonment was the culmination of a confrontation between an outspoken social media personality and Liberia’s highest court.

Before his incarceration, Prophet Key had become known for an aggressive style of commentary that frequently involved politicians, public officials, prominent personalities, and institutions.

His broadcasts attracted attention because of their directness and often confrontational tone. To his supporters, the style represented fearlessness and a willingness to speak about issues others avoided.

To his critics, however, some of his statements crossed the boundaries of responsible public criticism. The conflict with the judiciary ultimately became the most serious consequence of that approach.

The Supreme Court, sitting in its Full Bench, found Prophet Key guilty of criminal contempt on February 13, 2026, citing statements that it considered vulgar, insulting and abusive. Among the conduct considered by the Court were remarks involving the mother of Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay and allegations of corruption against members of the judiciary that the Court found unsupported by evidence. The decision sent Prophet Key from the world of online commentary into the highly restrictive environment of the Monrovia Central Prison.

When Expression Met the Authority of the Court

The case immediately raised questions beyond the fate of one individual. At its core was a difficult question for a democratic society: how far can an individual go in criticizing public institutions, particularly the judiciary, before criticism becomes punishable conduct?

Prophet Key’s supporters viewed the imprisonment through the lens of freedom of expression and argued that a strong democracy must tolerate harsh criticism, including criticism that may be uncomfortable or offensive.

The Supreme Court, however, approached the matter from the perspective of the authority and integrity of judicial proceedings. The Court acknowledged constitutional protections for freedom of expression but emphasized that those protections are accompanied by responsibilities.

The decision referenced Articles 5, 14 and 15 of Liberia’s 1986 Constitution while addressing the relationship between expression, individual rights, public order and national values.

The result was a sentence that effectively transformed the debate from an argument over what Prophet Key was allowed to say into a legal determination over the consequences of what he had said.

The Apology That Changed the Tone

Inside prison, Prophet Key eventually made a move that signaled a significant shift from the public persona that had brought him before the Supreme Court.

On July 28, he issued a handwritten apology. The document was addressed to Chief Justice Gbeisay, Associate Justices Yussif D. Kaba, Boakai N. Kanneh, Jamesetta H. Wolokolie and Ceaineh D. Clinton Johnson.

He also extended his apology to judges, magistrates and the judiciary generally. Most significantly, he acknowledged having accused members of the judiciary of corruption without proof.

He also apologized to Liberian women for statements he acknowledged were insulting. The apology was significant because it acknowledged the conduct at the center of the contempt proceedings.

It also suggested that Prophet Key understood that returning to freedom required more than simply waiting for the calendar to reach the end of his sentence.

But the apology created another question: Was writing the apology enough? According to the account of his supporters, the answer was no.

The Supreme Court did not reportedly limit its requirement to Prophet Key writing an apology. That meant the apology had to move from a document produced by Prophet Key to a public statement appearing in three local newspapers for five consecutive days.

A handwritten apology could remain a private or limited document. A newspaper publication, by contrast, would place the statement before the broader public and ensure that the acknowledgment of wrongdoing reached an audience beyond the courtroom.

According to a member of the Free Positive Movement, Abu A. Kamara efforts were made to have the requirement fulfilled, but publication schedules and other logistical issues reportedly created difficulties.

Some of the required publications allegedly did not appear within the expected timeframe, raising questions about whether the five-day requirement had been fully satisfied.

That uncertainty has now become one of the most important issues surrounding Prophet Key’s freedom. The Prophet Key case highlights a distinction that is easy to overlook when a person receives a fixed prison sentence. For Prophet Key’s family and supporters, the matter is no longer an abstract debate about legal conditions.

World.title: Liberia Must Not Become The Next Haiti – The Cocaine Crisis Is A National Security Emergency
World.content:
My fellow Liberians,

Today, I speak to you not merely as a lawyer. I speak as a Liberian citizen, as an educator, as a parent, and as a political leader who believes deeply that the survival and prosperity of the Liberian Republic depend upon the supremacy of the Constitution, the rule of law, accountable government, and institutions that serve the people rather than powerful individuals.

By Tiawan Saye Gongloe, SCL, contributing writer

Liberia is confronting a moment that we must not underestimate. What is unfolding following the discovery of enormous quantities of cocaine in our country is not simply a law-enforcement matter. It is not simply an LDEA matter, a police matter, or an airport-security matter. It is a national-security crisis, and if we fail to confront it comprehensively, it could become a threat to the very survival of the Liberian state.

Let us first appreciate the scale of what has happened. In June, Liberian authorities seized approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine at Roberts International Airport, reportedly valued at more than US$19 million. Then came the discovery of approximately 3,971 kilograms—nearly four metric tons—of cocaine in the Duazon area, with authorities estimating its value at approximately US$317 million. Reuters described the seizure as one of the largest recorded drug busts in Liberia.

My fellow Liberians, this is not the work of a few young people selling drugs on a street corner. The sheer volume and value point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise. We therefore have to ask who brought the drugs into Liberia, who received them, who transported them, who protected them, who knew about them, who facilitated their movement, who was paid, and, most importantly, whether anyone within the Liberian state helped make the operation possible.

These questions are no longer merely questions raised by ordinary citizens. They arise from statements made by officials within Liberia’s own security establishment. The Inspector General of Police has reportedly said that the cocaine operation was sanctioned at a very senior level of government and has referred to senior government officials in connection with the matter, without publicly identifying them. That is an extraordinarily serious statement. If the Inspector General has evidence that senior government officials were involved, the Liberian people deserve to know what the evidence establishes. If the evidence is not yet sufficient to identify anyone publicly, then those persons should be investigated through a process capable of establishing the truth.

Let me make one thing absolutely clear. I am not accusing any individual who has not been proven guilty. Every person accused of a crime is entitled to due process, and every accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty. That is the rule of law, and because I believe in the rule of law, I will not abandon it simply because the allegations before us are frightening.

But the rule of law does not mean that government should remain silent when credible allegations of criminal conduct reach into the highest levels of government. The rule of law requires a fearless, impartial and professional investigation. It requires evidence. It requires accountability. And where the evidence establishes criminal responsibility, it requires prosecution.

Indeed, the seriousness of this matter is demonstrated by the fact that senior police personnel have themselves come under scrutiny. Reports indicate that police officials and an NSA operative were detained or interrogated in connection with the investigation, while a senior police officer was removed from his position following an allegation that he accepted US$10,000 in connection with suspects in the cocaine case. Importantly, allegations remain allegations, and those accused are entitled to due process. But the involvement of personnel from institutions responsible for combating crime makes one thing clear: public confidence in Liberia’s security architecture is at stake.

I therefore want to acknowledge what President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has done so far. His administration has taken administrative and law-enforcement measures, including suspensions, dismissals, arrests, charges and detentions involving persons connected to the investigation. Senior security personnel have come under scrutiny, and the administration has demonstrated publicly that it intends to take the matter seriously.

For those actions, Mr. President, I say thank you. When a government takes action in the right direction, responsible citizens should acknowledge it.

But I must also say respectfully and firmly: Mr. President, this is not enough.

The scale of this crisis requires something more comprehensive. I therefore call upon President Boakai to establish a truly independent Commission of Inquiry into Liberia’s cocaine crisis and the broader narcotics-trafficking threat to the Republic.

I emphasize the word independent because if senior officials within the police, intelligence services, airport security, drug-enforcement institutions or other security agencies are themselves implicated or under investigation, the Liberian people cannot reasonably be expected to have complete confidence in an investigation conducted exclusively within the same institutional structures.

The Commission should include persons with expertise in criminal investigation, narcotics trafficking, financial intelligence, forensic accounting, money laundering, international organized crime, constitutional and criminal law, cybersecurity, border security and asset tracing. It should have appropriate legal authority to obtain documents and testimony, trace financial transactions, examine communications and movements relevant to the investigation, identify facilitators and beneficiaries, and make recommendations for criminal prosecution. Its findings should be made public, subject only to legitimate national-security limitations.

The central principle must be simple: follow the money.

Cocaine is the commodity. Money is the motive. Corruption is often the bridge between criminal money and legitimate institutions. Therefore, the investigation cannot stop with the cocaine itself. We must ask where the money went, who received it, who deposited it, who acquired property, who acquired businesses, who suddenly accumulated unexplained wealth, who provided protection, who made the critical telephone calls, who intervened, who gave instructions, and whether proceeds of narcotics trafficking entered Liberia’s legitimate economy or political system.

These questions should not be answered through rumor, political speculation or government propaganda. They must be answered through evidence.

My fellow Liberians, the cocaine crisis did not arrive in a vacuum. It has emerged in an environment in which corruption, weak institutions, impunity, unexplained wealth, allegations of illegal exploitation of natural resources, and disregard for accountability rules have repeatedly challenged the rule of law.

This is why I regard the cocaine crisis as a manifestation of a deeper governance crisis.

During an earlier Unity Party administration, the government itself described corruption as a vampire. The metaphor was appropriate. A vampire feeds quietly and survives by draining the life out of its victim. But look at what has happened since. The vampire did not die. Corruption became worse under the Coalition for Democratic Change, and today, under the Unity Party again, many Liberians have the perception that the vampire has become even more powerful.

This is not merely a political slogan. It is a question of the rule of law.

Consider, for example, the controversy surrounding the approximately US$10 million project in Foya, Lofa County. The government has explained that the structure is intended to serve as the Mano River Union Center for Regional Peace and Development rather than as a private presidential residence. But civil-society organizations and others have raised questions concerning its financing, procurement and transparency. The Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia has specifically called for full disclosure regarding the project.

The Liberian people therefore have legitimate questions. Was the project properly appropriated? Was it included in the national budget? Under what legal authority was the contract awarded? Was the procurement process consistent with the Public Procurement and Concessions Act? Was competitive procurement followed? Who financed the project? Where did the money come from? Who authorized the expenditure? Who contracted the project? And who will ultimately benefit?

I want to be absolutely clear: I am not saying that the Foya project is financed with drug money. I have no basis to make such an accusation without evidence. But in the midst of the largest narcotics investigation in Liberia’s history, the government should have no difficulty providing a complete and transparent account of the source of funds for a multimillion-dollar public project.

If the money is legitimate, transparency should establish that fact. If the procurement was lawful, the records should establish it. If the expenditure was properly authorized, the government should be able to demonstrate it.

And given the extraordinary cocaine investigation now before the country, Liberians are entitled to ask a broader question: could any unexplained source of money entering Liberia’s economy be drug money? That is not an accusation against the Foya project or any individual. It is a question that responsible government should answer through transparency and evidence.

The same principle applies to the troubling developments along the Liberia-Guinea border.

There have been reports and allegations concerning activities along the Makona River and claims relating to mineral extraction. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies has documented reports surrounding a border incident in which soldiers alleged that a company was extracting minerals, including gold and diamonds. Other reporting has raised allegations concerning illegal mining along the Makona River.

Again, I am not declaring those allegations to be established facts. But they deserve serious investigation.

Who is mining? Who owns the equipment? Who has the legal authority or concession? Who is exporting the minerals? Who is paying whom? Who is protecting the operations? Are Liberian minerals being illegally transported across the border? Are politically connected persons involved? And are any security personnel facilitating these activities?

These are legitimate questions because illegal mining is not simply an environmental problem. It can become a revenue problem, a corruption problem, a border-security problem and a national-security problem.

The government itself has recognized the seriousness of illicit mining and has moved toward stronger enforcement and interagency coordination. That is welcome. But the same principle applies here as in the cocaine investigation: follow the money and follow the evidence.

My fellow Liberians, there is another political issue that deserves reflection.

During the 2023 presidential campaign, President Boakai, then a presidential candidate, was reported to have said that he could “dance with the devil” if doing so would help him win the presidency.

I raise that statement today not because I am suggesting that President Boakai literally made a pact with the devil. I am certainly not suggesting that anything supernatural caused the cocaine crisis. I raise it because political language sometimes contains a warning that becomes more meaningful with time.

The “devil” in that statement can be understood as a metaphor for political compromise with people or forces whose conduct or values may be inconsistent with the principles of good governance.

There is an old warning: the devil never dances for free.

Every compromise with corruption has a price. Every accommodation with criminality has a price. Every political alliance built without regard to principle eventually sends the bill to somebody, and sometimes the bill is sent to the nation.

So today, I ask: What compromises were made in the pursuit of political power? Who were the people with whom political leaders had to dance? What did those people expect in return? What access did they receive? And is Liberia now paying the price for political compromises that should never have been made?

I am not accusing President Boakai of making any agreement with drug traffickers. I am not saying that the cocaine crisis is the consequence of his campaign statement. That would be irresponsible. I am asking a broader political question: When political expediency becomes more important than principle, who ultimately pays the price?

Because the real devil in Liberia is not a supernatural being. The real devil is corruption. The real devil is greed. The real devil is impunity. The real devil is political patronage. The real devil is the abuse of public office. The real devil is the belief that political connections are more powerful than the law. And if we allow those forces to become normalized, they will eventually threaten the Republic itself.

My fellow Liberians, this crisis is also fundamentally about our young people.

Liberia has a youthful population confronted by unemployment, poverty, limited opportunities and, in many communities, hopelessness. Into that environment comes an international narcotics industry with enormous financial resources. Drug traffickers can recruit, pay, corrupt and intimidate. They can offer young people money that legitimate employment cannot provide. That is dangerous. What happens when a young Liberian begins to believe that a drug dealer has more opportunities than a university graduate? What happens when legitimate work becomes less attractive than criminal enterprise? What happens when the young person begins to believe that the fastest route to wealth is through drugs, corruption or political connections?

That is how a nation loses its moral compass. We cannot allow that to happen.

The drug crisis must therefore be treated as an issue of education, employment, public health, youth development, criminal justice, border security and national security. Arrests alone will not solve it. We must destroy the economic ecosystem that makes narcotics profitable.

And this brings me to Haiti.

My fellow Liberians, I want to say something uncomfortable but necessary: Liberia must learn from Haiti.

Haiti is the first Black republic in the modern era. Liberia occupies a unique place in the history of Black statehood. Our histories are not identical, and I am not suggesting that Liberia is Haiti. But Haiti provides Liberia with a warning about what can happen when criminal organizations become stronger than state institutions.

Today, Haiti is experiencing a devastating crisis involving armed criminal groups, territorial control, trafficking, violence and weakened state authority. Liberia must never travel that road.

A country does not wake up one morning and discover that gangs control its streets. Institutional deterioration occurs gradually. Corruption becomes normal. Criminals purchase protection. Criminal networks penetrate institutions. Security officers become compromised. Young people are recruited. Criminal organizations acquire weapons and money. Political influence follows. Citizens lose confidence in government. And eventually, the state begins losing control.

That is the road Liberia must refuse to travel.

This is why the cocaine crisis must be understood as a national-security emergency.

Let me also speak politically.

For more than two decades, Liberians have watched the Unity Party and the Coalition for Democratic Change dominate national politics at different times. Different administrations have offered different slogans and different promises, but many of the same fundamental problems continue to return: corruption, impunity, weak institutions, political patronage, poverty and unemployment. Now we face the possibility that international narcotics networks have penetrated parts of Liberia’s security architecture.

I am not saying that every member of the Unity Party is corrupt. I am not saying that every member of the CDC is corrupt. That would be unfair and untrue. But political parties must accept responsibility for the systems that operate under their governments.

When corruption persists across successive administrations, it ceases to be merely an individual problem. It becomes a governance problem.

And the cocaine crisis is another manifestation of what has become normalized in Liberia: uncontrollable greed and endemic corruption.

Too many people have come to believe that public office is a pathway to personal enrichment. Too many believe government is a marketplace where influence can be purchased. Too many believe political connections can protect them from the law. That culture must end.

Government is a place to serve, not to steal. Governance is for the people, not the pockets.

My fellow Liberians, let us connect the issues. Corruption is a rule-of-law issue. Narcotics trafficking is a rule-of-law issue. Money laundering is a rule-of-law issue. Illegal mining is a rule-of-law issue. Procurement violations are a rule-of-law issue. Border insecurity is a national-security issue. The compromise of security officers is a national-security issue.

When these things begin appearing together, we must ask whether the institutions of the Republic themselves are being weakened.

That is why this crisis cannot be allowed to become another headline that eventually disappears.

The cocaine may be destroyed. The suspects may eventually be convicted or acquitted. But the system that allowed such an enormous criminal enterprise to operate in Liberia must be examined.

Mr. President, follow the money.

Follow the cocaine money. Follow suspicious financial transactions. Follow unexplained wealth. Follow properties and businesses. Follow bank accounts. Follow airport records. Follow immigration records. Follow shipping records. Follow relevant communications. Follow political relationships. Follow the chain of command. And follow the evidence wherever it leads.

If the evidence leads to a poor man, investigate him. If it leads to a police officer, investigate him. If it leads to a businessman, investigate him. If it leads to a minister, investigate him. If it leads to a legislator, investigate him. If it leads to a presidential appointee, investigate him. And if the evidence leads to someone close to the President, investigate him.

No one should be above the law.

Not because we want to destroy people, but because we want to save Liberia.

And after investigation must come prosecution where the evidence warrants it.

The purpose of an investigation is not to generate headlines. It is to establish facts. Once the facts are established, the law must follow. If the evidence establishes trafficking, prosecute. If it establishes money laundering, prosecute. If it establishes corruption, prosecute. If it establishes obstruction of justice, prosecute. If it establishes abuse of public office to facilitate criminal conduct, prosecute.

And if the evidence establishes innocence, clear the innocent. That is justice.

To the Liberian people, I say: do not allow this crisis to become merely another partisan argument. Do not ask first whether the matter involves the Unity Party, the CDC or the LPP. Ask whether Liberia is safe. Ask whether our children are safe. Ask whether our institutions are safe. Ask whether our security institutions can be trusted. Ask who is protecting the drug traffickers. Ask where the money is going. And ask who benefits.

This is not merely a political question.

It is a Liberian question.

The Liberian People’s Party must stand on the side of Liberia. We will not defend criminals because they belong to our party. We will not condemn innocent people because they belong to another party. We will defend one fundamental principle: every person is equal before the law.

To the young people of Liberia, I say: do not allow drug traffickers to purchase your future. Do not become couriers. Do not become distributors. Do not become protectors of criminal enterprises. Do not allow someone else’s greed to destroy your life.

There is nothing glamorous about cocaine. There is nothing heroic about addiction. There is nothing powerful about destroying another person’s future.

The real power is education. The real power is discipline. The real power is honest work. The real power is building a Liberia where a young person does not have to become a criminal to become successful.

And government has an obligation to build that Liberia.

Mr. President, you came to office promising integrity. You promised accountability. You promised to fight corruption. You promised to restore confidence in government. You now have an historic opportunity to demonstrate that those promises mean something.

Do not allow this crisis to become another scandal that disappears when the headlines disappear. Do not allow a few low-level actors to be sacrificed while powerful actors remain untouched. Do not allow Liberia to become a country where the small fish go to prison while the big fish negotiate their freedom.

Establish the independent Commission of Inquiry.

Make it genuinely independent.

Give it the necessary authority.

Give it access to the evidence.

Let it follow the money.

Let it identify the facilitators.

Let it identify the protectors.

Let it identify the beneficiaries.

Let it expose the networks.

And let the courts do their constitutional duty.

If the evidence proves guilt, prosecute.

If the evidence proves innocence, clear the innocent.

But do not hide the truth.

Liberia deserves the truth. Our children deserve the truth. Our security institutions deserve the truth. And the Republic of Liberia deserves nothing less than the truth.

My fellow Liberians, this cocaine crisis is a test. It is a test of President Boakai. It is a test of the Liberia National Police. It is a test of the LDEA. It is a test of the National Security Agency. It is a test of the Ministry of Justice. It is a test of our courts. It is a test of the Legislature. It is a test of our political parties. But above all, it is a test of the Liberian nation.

We survived civil war. We survived Ebola. We survived political instability. We must not now lose Liberia to organized crime.

We must not wait until criminals become stronger than the institutions of the Republic. We must not wait until our young people become the foot soldiers of international drug cartels. We must not wait until corruption destroys the remaining moral authority of government. And we must not wait until Liberia begins resembling countries where criminal organizations control communities and governments struggle to reclaim their own territory.

Liberia must not become Haiti.

The warning signs must be confronted while they are still warning signs.

Mr. President, establish the independent Commission of Inquiry. Let the investigation be independent, professional and comprehensive. Let it follow the money. Let it follow the evidence. Let it identify the networks, the protectors and the beneficiaries. And let justice follow wherever the evidence leads.

If the evidence proves guilt, prosecute. If the evidence proves innocence, clear the innocent. But do not hide the truth.

The cocaine may be seized. The cocaine may be destroyed. But the lesson must not be destroyed with it.

Let us destroy the cocaine, but let us also destroy the culture of impunity that permits criminal enterprises to flourish. Let us destroy the belief that public office is personal property. Let us destroy the belief that political connections place anyone above the law. Let us confront greed and endemic corruption. Let us restore the rule of law.

Because the real national emergency is not merely the cocaine we have discovered.

It is the system that made it possible for nearly four metric tons of cocaine to be found in Liberia.

And the question before us is therefore not simply, “Who brought the drugs?”

The deeper questions are: Who opened the door? Who protected the door? Who benefited from the door being open? And who has the power to close it permanently?

Liberia must answer those questions, and Liberia must answer them now.

If we do not control the criminals, the criminals may eventually control us. If we do not defeat corruption, corruption may eventually defeat the Republic. And if we do not protect our young people, we will lose the future of Liberia.

Government is a place to serve, not to steal. Governance is for the people, not the pockets. Let us sweep corruption away, defend the rule of law, protect our children, protect our Republic, and build a better Liberia.

Thank you.

May God bless the Republic of Liberia, and may God protect the Liberian people.

A Better Liberia is possible

World.title: Nine Arrested in Matero Over Polling Agent Murder
World.content:
THE Zambia Police Service has confirmed multiple arrests following isolated incidents during and after the August 13 General Elections.

In Matero, Lusaka Province, nine suspects have been arrested in connection with the alleged murder of 57-year-old polling agent LOVEMORE CHISHIMA.

Mr. CHISHIMA was allegedly assaulted at Kasamba Polling Station and later died.

According to a statement issued by Inspector General of Police GRAPHEL MUSAMBA, the suspects are in police custody as investigations continue.

In a separate incident, police arrested six men allegedly found in possession of offensive weapons, 22 rounds of ammunition and a Toyota Land Cruiser.

Police say they are seeking SEAN TEMBO to assist with investigations.

Meanwhile, in Kalomo, Southern Province, one suspect was arrested following an incident in which four people were assaulted, with one victim sustaining a gunshot wound.

Police recovered a firearm and ammunition.

In Kasama, Northern Province, police are also investigating an attack on the residence of Acting Permanent Secretary BEAUTY UNDI-PHIRI, allegedly carried out by armed supporters of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity.

One suspect has since been apprehended.

Mr. MUSAMBA says although the overall conduct of the elections was peaceful, police are taking the reported incidents seriously.

He has warned against incitement, unlawful activities and the spread of false information, while urging citizens to remain calm and allow the Electoral Commission of Zambia to professionally manage and announce the election results.

World.title: ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review
World.content:
ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has lifted, with immediate effect, its suspension of the counting and announcement of results in the 2026 general election, and says the first set of results will be announced at 22:00 tonight.

ECZ Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis told a press briefing on Friday that a review of the security situation, carried out in consultation with law enforcement agencies, found that the threat to the electoral process had been contained and that measures were now in place to allow counting to resume.

The Commission had earlier suspended counting and the announcement of results nationwide after reports of violence directed at polling staff and, in some instances, the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes. That suspension was to be reviewed within 24 hours depending on the security situation.

“Following a review of the security situation and consultations with the relevant law enforcement agencies, I am pleased to inform you and to inform the nation that the security threat to the electoral process has been contained,” Zaloumis said.

She said polling had been successfully conducted at all polling stations across the country, with the last station closing in the early hours of Friday at 02:00.

“We therefore wish to advise all stakeholders that the suspension of the counting and announcement of results has been lifted, with immediate effect,” she said.

Zaloumis appealed to political parties, candidates, their supporters and members of the public to remain peaceful and allow polling staff to work without interference, intimidation or violence. She said the safety of polling staff, the security of electoral materials and the integrity of the process remained paramount, and that law enforcement agencies would continue providing security as counting and the announcement of results proceed.

She reminded the nation that official results are only those announced by the ECZ in accordance with prescribed procedures, and warned candidates against self-declaration.

“It is an offence under Section 89(1) of the Electoral Process Amendment Act No. 32 of 2021 for any person without lawful authority to announce and declare the results of an election,” she said, urging all presidential and other candidates to desist from declaring themselves winners and to allow the Commission to complete its constitutional duty of counting, verifying and announcing results.

Zaloumis thanked Zambians for their patience and cooperation, acknowledged the work of law enforcement in maintaining order, and commended ECZ staff for their commitment to duty. She said the Commission would continue to update the nation as the process progresses, and that stakeholders were invited to join at 22:00 as the first results begin to stream in.

The suspension, and now its lifting, come after opposition leader Brian Mundubile declared himself the winner of the presidential election on Friday, citing his alliance’s parallel vote tabulation, a claim that remains a Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance position rather than an official result. President Hakainde Hichilema had called on Zambians to remain calm as the count continued.

World.title: HICHILEMA SAYS EARLY ELECTION RESULTS ENCOURAGING
World.content:
PRESIDENT HAKAINDE HICHILEMA says he has continued to receive encouraging results following yesterday’s voting.

President HICHILEMA says he has also received reports of peace, unity and solidarity across the country as the counting process continues.

In a statement posted on his Facebook page, President HICHILEMA has urged Zambians to remain peaceful, patient and patriotic while awaiting the official results from the Electoral Commission of Zambia — ECZ.

Meanwhile, UPND National Management Committee representative MULAMBO HAIMBE says early indications from tallying centres are encouraging for President HICHILEMA.

Mr. HAIMBE says reported trends point to a strong performance for the incumbent, with high voter turnout recorded in Southern, Western and North-Western Provinces.

He says the picture in Central Province is favourable, while the party is also seeing gains in Northern Province.

However, Mr. HAIMBE has stressed that the information being shared represents early indications and not official election results.

He says only the ECZ has the constitutional authority to declare the winner of the presidential election.

Mr. HAIMBE has further cautioned political parties and members of the public against circulating unverified claims of victory, saying the ECZ should be allowed to complete the process of collation, verification and announcement of results.

The UPND has since called on citizens to exercise patience and restraint and respect the conclusion of the democratic process.

World.title: Ex-ZBF boss Chileshe hails bronze medal winning boxers
World.content:
Former Zambia Boxing Federation President Thomas Chileshe has hailed Team Zambia’s boxers for securing the country’s only two medals at the just-ended Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

Team Zambia’s entire medal haul came from the ring, with Catherine Mwape and Emmanuel Katema, both claiming bronze.

Mwape made history as the first Zambian female boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal after reaching the semi-finals of the Women’s 54kg division. She lost to India’s Preeti Preeti.

Katema added a second bronze in the men’s 65kg category following a hard-fought semi-final defeat to England’s Patris Mughalzai.

Speaking in Ndola, Chileshe said winning at the Commonwealth Games is never easy.

“The boxers have done well. We cannot complain. Moreover, it is not easy to get a medal at the Commonwealth Games. I know we couldn’t get gold like we did in Manchester in 2002. It is not a failure, it is an achievement.”

The former ZBF chief reminded Zambians of the country’s rich boxing pedigree on the Commonwealth stage, citing past legends.

“From the archive Zambia is very strong in boxing. This is a testament and a fact about Zambia and boxing, let’s look back to the time of Lottie Mwale, Charm ‘Shuffle’ Chiteule or even the time of Kennedy Kanyanta, we are very talented in boxing.”

Zambia’s boxing history at the Games includes historic gold medals from Lottie Mwale in 1974 and recent podium finishes such as silver and bronze at Birmingham 2022.

Chileshe, however, urged the medalists not to get comfortable.

“Our boxers should not wear the pride for now until they achieve greater things. If they relax, pride will drop them down. Let them reach the sky.”

World.title: ECZ Suspends Counting and Announcement of Results
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia — ECZ — has with immediate effect suspended the counting and announcement of election results across the country.

The Commission says the decision follows reports of violence during the counting and announcement of results in some districts.

In a press release issued today, ECZ Chairperson MWANGALA ZALOUMIS said the violence has targeted polling staff and, in some cases, resulted in the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes.

Mrs. ZALOUMIS said the suspension has been necessitated by the prevailing security situation and continued threats of violence.

She said the decision has been made in accordance with Section 67, Subsection 3 of the Electoral Process Act Number 35 of 2016.

The ECZ Chairperson said the Commission will review the suspension within 24 hours.

The suspension means the counting and announcement of results will remain on hold until the Commission makes a further determination.

World.title: Shibuyunji election results pour in
World.content:
Elections results from 18 out of 33 polling stations for Mwembezhi East Constituency in Shibuyunji district have been verified and announced.

As of 08:00 hours today, the totaling centre had received results from Makombwe, Nampeya, Nampundwe, Sala and Chikonka Ward respectively.

ZANIS reports that Mwembezhi East Returning Officer Sitali Muwanei said so far United Party for National Development (UPND) Presidential candidate Hakainde Hichilema has garnered 6, 175 votes followed by National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Peace (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile with 912 votes.

The returning officer noted that only results for Presidential candidates have been verified and announced.

Mr Muwanei explained that results are still coming from the remaining polling stations and will be announced as they arrive.

He has urged stakeholders to exercise patience as they wait for results.

World.title: Mbala receives poll results
World.content:
bala Central Constituency has continued receiving results from various polling stations following the closure of polls last night.

The totaling centre has so far received results from 25 out of the 52 polling stations in the constituency.

According to the latest figures, at Presidential level, National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile is leading with 3,746 votes, while United Party for National Development (UPND) candidate Hakainde Hichilema has polled 2,857 votes.

World.title: ECZ announces NRPUP lead in Lusangazi
World.content:
National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Peace (NRPUP) Candidate Banda Festone has taken an early lead in the Ukwimi Ward race in Lusangazi Central Constituency after polling 785 votes from 5 of the 6 polling stations tallied, the Electoral Commission of Zambia has announced.

According to the ECZ record of proceeding at the totalling of votes announced yesterday, August 13, 2026, a total of 1,619 ballot papers were recorded covering Kasangazi Primary School-01, Sandwe Local Court-01, Songovwa Community School-01, Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-01 and Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-02 centres.

Of the total votes cast, 26 ballots were rejected.

Festone Banda, led the race with 785 votes, followed by United Party for National Development (UPND)’s Phiri Enala with 655 votes, while Citizens First’s Mapeti Paul garnered 106 votes.

Mr Banda got his highest figure at Kasangazi Primary School-01 with 238 votes and at Songowe Community School-01 with 190 votes.

He also polled 160 votes at Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-01 and 149 votes at Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-02.

Ms Phiri led at Sandwe Local Court-01 with 138 votes and at Songowe Community School-01 with 183 votes.

Mapeti Paul’s highest return was 94 votes at Songowe Community School-01.

The totalling of results for the remaining one polling station in Ukwimi Ward is expected to be complete later today in accordance with The Electoral Process Act, No. 35 of 2016 and The Electoral Process (General) Regulations, 2021.

Final results for Ukwimi Ward Councillor will be announced once all 6 polling stations have been tallied and verified.
