Other demands include a five-day work week in banks, filling vacancies in government services and public establishments, convening the Indian Labour Conference and restoring OPS.

BMS has also reiterated its opposition to several provisions of the Industrial Relations Code and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, arguing that they could weaken workers' rights, job security and social security. It has sought formal consultations between the Centre and central trade unions before amendments are made.

The organisation also wants the Centre and states to reconsider the status of more than one crore âscheme workersâ, saying many work 10-12 hours a day but remain outside effective labour-law and social-security protection.

World.title: Govt scraps 12-minute ad cap for TV channel
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Television channels will no longer be restricted to 12 minutes of s per hour, with the government deciding to scrap the two-decade-old cap in a move it says will put traditional broadcasters on a more level footing with digital platforms.The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the Gazette, the information and broadcasting ministry said.The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 TV channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now. Cable television, then the dominant distribution platform, was largely analog and offered limited capacity and consumer choice.With digitisation, platforms including cable TV, direct-to-home, HITS and IPTV can now carry 300 to 500 channels or more, significantly expanding viewer choice and competition, the ministry said.The decision could give broadcasters greater flexibility to determine advertising inventory, an important consideration for an industry that remains heavily dependent on advertising revenue across both pay and free-to-air channels.The ministry also cited the growing competition television faces from digital media, where there is no comparable statutory cap on advertising duration.It said the existing restriction had created a ânon-level playing fieldâ for conventional television broadcasters and that removing it would promote âfair competitionâ and ease of doing business.The change, however, will become operational only from the date the amendment to the Cable Television Networks Rules is formally notified.

World.title: Pew survey: What US, UK and others think about India at 80
World.content:
As India completes 79 years of independence, its global standing presents a striking study in contrasts.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted across 36 countries between February and May 2026 reveals an international community divided down the middle: a global median of 45% of respondents hold a favorable view of India, while 41% express an unfavorable opinion.



Behind this median lies a complex tapestry of geopolitical shifts, historical rivalries, and evolving regional alliances.

From enthusiasm in Western Europe and East Africa to frosty hostility in parts of the Middle East and South Asia, public perception of the worldâs most populous democracy depends heavily on where you ask.

Neighbourhood contrasts & global scorecard

Nowhere is this divergence more intense than in India's immediate backyard.

While proximity can foster cooperation, in South Asia it has produced antithetical attitudes.

Sri Lanka has the most favourable view of India, with 79% of adults expressing a positive opinion.

Pakistan sits at the opposite end, with just 7% viewing India favourably. The gulf between the two countries reflects decades of conflict, political rivalry and competing national narratives.

Turkey is another major outlier. Only 15% of Turks have a favourable opinion of India, while a majority hold an unfavourable view.





In the West Bank and East Jerusalem, just 18% express a positive opinion.

Yet beyond these pockets of hostility, India finds considerable goodwill across much of the world.

as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?

Kenya and the United Kingdom rank alongside Sri Lanka among the countries most positive towards India, with roughly seven in 10 adults expressing favourable views.

Majorities in Germany, Israel, Italy, Sweden, Japan and Thailand also see India positively.

In contrast, Latin American publics express mixed-to-negative views, alongside substantial shares of respondents who offer no opinion.

The findings suggest that India's global image is not simply a reflection of its diplomatic alliances.

Economic ties, strategic partnerships, cultural familiarity and perceptions of India's growing global role all appear to shape how people view the country.

India's image is changing

The bigger story is perhaps not where India stands today, but how its image has changed.

In most countries surveyed, opinions have remained relatively stable since Pew last asked the question. But in 10 countries, the change has been statistically significant â and in seven of them, India's favourability has fallen.

Turkey and Nigeria have recorded the sharpest declines since 2025, with the share of people expressing a favourable opinion of India falling by 10 percentage points in both countries.

India has also lost ground in the United States, Indonesia, South Africa and Mexico.

The decline is particularly striking in Bangladesh.

Pew's previous survey there was conducted in 2024. Since then, the share of Bangladeshis with a favourable opinion of India has fallen by 15 percentage points, leaving fewer than half with a positive view.

At the same time, the number of Bangladeshis who do not express an opinion has also fallen sharply, from 24% to just 7%. In other words, more Bangladeshis now appear to have a defined opinion of India â and that opinion has become considerably less favourable.

The trend is not uniformly negative, however.

India's image has improved significantly in Germany, Britain and Sri Lanka.

The share of Britons with a favourable opinion of India has risen 11 points since 2025, while Germany has recorded a six-point increase. Sri Lanka has seen an even bigger jump, with favourability rising 14 points since 2024.

Looking further back to 2023 reveals another interesting divide.

Across several European countries, India's image has strengthened substantially since the first post-pandemic survey.

In Germany, for example, only 47% had a favourable opinion of India in 2023. That figure has now climbed to 63%.

France has followed a similar trajectory. India's favourability there has risen from 39% in 2023 to 50% today.

Outside Europe, however, the picture is less encouraging.

South Korea is one example. In 2023, 59% of South Koreans viewed India favourably. Today, that figure has dropped to 44%.

Latin America also tends to lean more negative, although large numbers of people in several European and Latin American countries do not express an opinion at all.

Politics matters too

India's global image is also shaped by domestic political ideology in some countries.

The United States and Canada show a striking pattern: people on the political left are more likely than conservatives to view India favourably.

In the US, 54% of liberals express a positive opinion of India, compared with 40% of conservatives. In Canada, the corresponding figures are 58% and 45%.

Israel presents almost the exact opposite picture.

There, 68% of people on the political right view India favourably, compared with just 46% on the left.

The ideological divide underlines how perceptions of India can be tied not only to India's own policies, but also to how different political constituencies interpret its role in the world.

A mixed but largely positive global image

So, as India enters its 80th year as an independent nation, what does the world think of it?

The answer is neither uniformly celebratory nor overwhelmingly negative.

Pakistan and Turkey may give India the stink eye, but they represent the more hostile end of a much broader spectrum.

From Sri Lanka and Kenya to Britain, Germany and Israel, India enjoys strong positive sentiment in several strategically important countries.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

At the same time, the declines in Bangladesh, the US, South Korea, Turkey, Nigeria and other countries show that India's global image cannot be taken for granted.

India's international reputation is therefore becoming more consequential â and more contested.

As New Delhi seeks a larger role in global affairs, its challenge will not simply be to build economic and military power, but also to shape how that power is perceived abroad.

At 80, India is increasingly a country the world has an opinion about.

World.title: Sunil Amrith On 'The Burning Earth' And The Unequal Costs Of Environmental Destruction
World.content:
Sunil Amrith is the Renu and Anand Dhawan Professor of History at Yale University with a secondary appointment as professor at the Yale School of the Environment. He serves as Director of the Macmillan Centre for International and Area Studies and Yale's Vice Provost for International Affairs.

He has received the 2016 Infosys Prize in Humanities, a 2017 MacArthur Fellowship, and the 2025 Toynbee Prize in Global History, among others. He has authored five books that put Asia at the heart of global history. In this conversation, he discusses his book, 'The Burning Earth'.

Excerpts from the interview.

Q: Why did you feel this book needed to be written?

A:

It was a coming together of my academic life and the rest of my life.

For close to 20 years, I had been researching some of the themes that do make it into 'The Burning Earth'. I've particularly been interested in the relationship between migration, the movement of people and environmental change. So I wrote a book more than 10 years ago called 'Crossing the Bay of Bengal', which I think was my first foray into environmental history, in which I was really thinking about the enormous movement of people, particularly from Tamil Nadu, to southeast Asia in the 19th and 20th century, many of them to work on rubber plantations, but also to work in port cities, places like Singapore and Penang and Rangoon, and understanding that that was actually a moment of fundamental transformation in the environment.





.. At the same time, as a teacher, but also as a parent, as a citizen, the climate crisis became quite unavoidable in my own consciousness. And so for me, that prompted me to scale things up beyond my areas of specialisation towards perhaps the biggest question, which is how did we get to this point of planetary crisis? And that's really what's at the heart of 'The Burning Earth'.

Q: You also bring in a kind of storytelling which positions itself in different geographies as if to say, the inherited narratives of Eurocentric histories are not what we're going to look at.

A:

If the question is what is it about my own perspective that may make this book a little bit different from some of the other books out there on this big theme of the environment, it is the fact that my own training is not in European and North American history. And I think most of what is called global history continues to take as its starting point and as its default, a kind of familiar North Atlantic history. And so by starting the book in China and ending it in Indonesia, I was really trying to write it anchored in Asia.

.. Asia has always been home to the majority of humanity. It still is today. And so it seemed to me completely fitting to really think about the history of this planet with a firm anchor in the part of the world, the part of the planet which has been the most inhabited by most people throughout the longest period of time.

Q: How do you bring in a methodology which ensures that what you're positioning and presenting can be as accurate as possible?

A:

That's the biggest challenge of a book like this. There's no possibility that I can have the primary expertise in all of these areas that I write about in the book.

And so in some ways that was a leap that I took. Academia is a collective enterprise. And this is very much a book that builds on my own work in some areas. And in other areas, it's really sort of bringing together my reading in multiple fields of scholarship and different disciplines as well.

So I'm a historian, but some of the most exciting new scholarship which I draw on and interpret is actually coming from the physical sciences.There's some phenomenally interesting work in paleoclimatology, for example, which is trying to reconstruct past climates using ice cores, using lake bed sediment, using tree rings.

And of course, these disciplines traditionally and even still within the walls of the university barely meet. But what's been very interesting about recent work on climate and environment in particular, is you have this forcing together of completely different ideas of what the archive is.

Q: You use the word 'elite' a few times when you're talking about social stratification for a very specific economic growth touted as well-being of a community, but usually you see it as exploitative.

A:

I don't use the word that many times, but when I do, I think it's doing a lot of work for me. 'The Burning Earth' is not an activist book, which is to say that it is just that bit muddier and less clear about the villains of the piece than activist writing necessarily has to be. And yet there is such a strong core in my own thinking of awareness of just how stark environmental inequalities are and just how much the scale of planetary destruction that has been achieved over the last two centuries has been disproportionately, not exclusively, but disproportionately driven by the elite pursuit of luxuries and of accumulation.

.. There is a story of human need in this book and there's also a story of human greed... I think we need to think about desire, we need to think about states, we need to think about liberation, we need to think about the genuinely liberatory promises that led to some of this environmental destruction which can't be reduced to a question of greed or even of capitalism...

There's no question that the social and economic system that has been a driving force in the climate crisis is the capitalist system.

But the socialist system in some sense was even more environmentally profligate and wasteful. It was just less successful. And so in terms of its longevity, in terms of the scale on which it was operating, it kind of doesn't compare with what a particular capitalist mode of production does to our ability to treat all of nature as commodity and to lead to this kind of constantly expanding frontier of production.

But my question is really a different one, which is, where were the alternatives? Who was thinking differently?

Q: You point out that there are these rather horrific incidents which are almost genocidal.

A:

I think that's one of the key narratives in the book to show that the moments of the most intensive and accelerated environmental destruction over the last several hundred years have almost always gone together with moments of intense violence. And violence is at the core of 'The Burning Earth'. Not just violence against the earth or against nature, but against other people... Wars that are going on all around us in the world today are part of a very long pattern where armed violence and militarism and military destruction have been inextricably bound with massive environmental destruction.

World.title: 'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
World.content:
Nearly eight decades after the 1947 Partition of British India gave birth to two independent nations, deep-seated historical trauma, and territorial disputes that have led to multiple military confrontations continue to shape the mindset of citizens on both sides of the border.

As the two countries celebrate their independence, a major survey by the Pew Research Center reveals that an overwhelming majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat.

Conducted across South Asia between February and May 2026, the findings highlight a persistent, deep-rooted mutual hostility that shows little sign of thawing. These sentiments reflect not merely political disagreements, but deeply entrenched unfavourable opinions among general populations, extending into perceptions of global superpowers, regional allies, and the long-term prospects for bilateral peace.

' Greatest threat ': India and Pakistan point at each other

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country.

Conversely, 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat.

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%. For Pakistanis, Israel and the US each register at 24% as major threats â though still far below India.

These threat perceptions align closely with how each public judges the otherâs commitment to peace.





Most Indians believe their own government and people are committed to good bilateral relations, but a majority say Pakistanâs government and people are not.

Pakistanis mirror this: they express confidence in their own sideâs commitment but doubt Indiaâs.

Mutual hostility runs deep

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Nearly nine in 10 Pakistanis have an unfavourable view of India, with 73% describing their opinion as 'very unfavourable'.

The sentiment cuts across demographic groups, suggesting that hostility toward India is not confined to any particular section of Pakistani society.

The picture in India is similarly bleak. As many as 78% of Indians have an unfavourable view of Pakistan, including 65% who hold a very unfavourable opinion. There is, however, a notable internal divide in India. Indian Muslims are somewhat more favorable toward Pakistan (21%) than Indian Hindus (6%), and they are also less likely to name Pakistan as their top threat (34% vs 57% among Hindus).

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Pew's polling also shows that this is not a temporary shift in sentiment.

Indian views of Pakistan have remained overwhelmingly negative for more than a decade, with the share expressing a favourable opinion never rising above 20% since 2013.

Historical Pew surveys also show that Pakistanis have long held predominantly negative views of India. Pakistani respondents expressing favourable views of India have generally ranged from single digits to around one-third.

Lack of trust

The survey further suggests that hostility is not simply about how Indians and Pakistanis perceive each other. It also extends to whether they believe the other side genuinely wants better relations.

A clear pattern emerges: people tend to believe that their own government and population are committed to good bilateral relations, while doubting the intentions of the other side.

When asked whether the Indian and Pakistani governments and people are committed to good relations with each other, the clear pattern is that people only have faith in their own country Pew Research report

A majority of Indians believe both the Indian government and Indian people are committed to maintaining good relations with Pakistan.

But a majority of Pakistanis reject that assessment, saying the Indian government and people are not committed to good relations.

The mirror image appears in Pakistan.

Beneath the geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.

A majority of Pakistanis say their government and people want good relations with India.

Most Indians, however, believe Pakistan's government and people are not committed to improving ties. About a quarter of Indian respondents were unsure.

This mutual lack of trust creates a difficult cycle: each side sees itself as willing to improve relations while viewing the other as unwilling to reciprocate.

Indian Muslims again stand apart to some degree. Around a third say the Pakistani government and people are committed to good relations, significantly higher than the corresponding share among Indian Hindus.

How Bangladesh, Sri Lanka view the rivals

The Pew findings become even more revealing when India and Pakistan are placed alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

Of the four South Asian countries surveyed, Sri Lanka is the only country that receives more positive than negative ratings from respondents in all three of the others.

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations.

India, meanwhile, has the widest range of perceptions.

Sri Lankans are overwhelmingly positive toward India, with 79% expressing a favourable opinion. In Bangladesh, 42% view India favourably. In Pakistan, however, the figure plunges to just 7%.

India is also seen as Sri Lanka's most important ally by a clear majority: 63% of Sri Lankan respondents name India.

The picture is very different in Bangladesh and Pakistan, where India is most often identified as the greatest threat.

Views of Prime Minister Narendra Modi follow a broadly similar pattern. Seventy percent of Sri Lankans express confidence in PM Modi to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 42% in Bangladesh and 4% in Pakistan.

The survey also finds that Pakistan is not universally viewed negatively across South Asia.

Fifty-seven percent of Sri Lankans and 54% of Bangladeshis have a favourable opinion of Pakistan, compared with only 8% of Indians.

Bangladesh itself receives broadly positive views in Pakistan and Sri Lanka: 66% of Pakistanis and 56% of Sri Lankans express favourable opinions of Bangladesh. Only about a quarter of Indians do so.

Sri Lanka emerges as the region's relative outlier. Around half or more of respondents in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh view the island nation positively, while significantly fewer hold negative views.

Divergent worldviews

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations to the way each country views the global order.

For Indians, Russia remains a particularly important and popular partner. Thirty-six percent identify Russia as India's most important ally, while 16% name the United States.

Russia's favourable image in India is particularly striking. Fifty-eight percent of Indians have a favourable opinion of Russia, while 51% express confidence in Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Pakistanis are considerably less positive: 39% have a favourable view of Russia and only 32% express confidence in Putin.

India's relationship with the United States is also reflected in public opinion. Indians are substantially more favourable toward the US than Pakistanis are and are more likely to express confidence in US President Donald Trump.

The picture is almost completely reversed when it comes to China.

An overwhelming 90% of Pakistanis have a favourable view of China, while 83% express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Three-quarters of Pakistanis identify China as their country's most important ally.

Saudi Arabia is a distant second, named by 12%.

In India, however, only around a quarter of respondents view China or Xi positively. Even Indian Muslims, who are more favourable toward China than Indian Hindus, remain negative toward both China and its president on balance.
