World.title: UAE Coal Deal Highlights Why Foreign Investors Are Betting on Kazakh Coal Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – A United Arab Emirates company has secured a 25-year license to develop the Kenderlyk coal deposit in eastern Kazakhstan, expanding foreign investment in the country’s mining sector.

According to documents released ahead of public hearings in early August, MQ Emirates Group Ltd will develop Coal-Shale Field No. 1 of the Kenderlyk deposit using open-pit mining methods.

Coal production is scheduled to begin in 2028, following geological exploration and preparatory work planned for 2026 and 2027. Initial output is projected at 10,000 metric tons, increasing to the mine’s planned annual capacity of 50,000 metric tons by 2034. Recoverable reserves are estimated at 940,000 metric tons.

The Kenderlyk deposit is located around 70 kilometers from the town of Zaisan in the East Kazakhstan Region. It has been known since the late 19th century, when coal and oil shale were extracted through small surface mines. During the Soviet era, the area underwent extensive geological exploration for coal, shale, and hydrocarbons.

Several years ago, the Kazakh Industry Ministry offered parts of the Kenderlyk deposit for auction. According to the National Geological Service, the broader deposit contains 11.3 million metric tons of coal reserves across three coal-bearing formations. Coal at Field No. 1 has a relatively high ash content of 35% to 40%.

Coal remains key to energy security

Although many countries are accelerating the shift toward renewable energy, coal remains one of the world’s primary sources of electricity. It generates roughly one-third of global power. Demand continues to be driven largely by China and India. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan ranks 10th globally in proven coal reserves, with an estimated 33.6 billion metric tons, enough to sustain current production levels for more than three centuries.

The country’s largest coal-producing regions include the Karagandy and Turgai coal basins in central Kazakhstan and the Ekibastuz, Maikuben and Karazhyra deposits in the northeast. Kazakhstan exports coal primarily to Russia, Poland, Uzbekistan, Türkiye, India and Malaysia.

To support future growth, the Energy Ministry plans to auction 10 additional coal exploration blocks by the end of the year. The government has also approved the Coal Power Development national project, which includes investment projects with a combined installed capacity of around 7.8 gigawatts.

Investment in the sector continues to rise. Mining companies invested 305 billion tenge (US$654 million) in 2025, while investment is projected to increase to 553 billion tenge (US$1.2 billion) this year.

Kazakhstan is also expanding investment in its broader mining sector. The government plans to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits, among the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten reserves, into the country’s first full-cycle tungsten operation.

Highly concentrated market

While Kazakhstan is expanding coal production, a new report from the Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition (APDC) found that the country’s primary wholesale coal market remains highly concentrated.

The agency’s review of the 2024-25 market concluded that the sector continues to be dominated by a small number of producers operating in an essentially unchanged oligopolistic market. For coal supplied to households and municipal utilities, the ERG Group and Karazhyra company controlled a combined market share of 74.8% in 2024 and 67.9% in 2025.

In the power generation segment, Bogatyr Komir and Kazakhmys Coal accounted for 84.1% of the market in 2024 and 81.6% in 2025. For industrial coal, the ERG Group held a market share of 62.3% in 2024, increasing to 69.1% in 2025. The agency said Kazakhstan’s oligopolistic market structure has contributed to sustained price increases.

According to APDC, wholesale prices for coal supplied to households increased 30% to 35% between 2022 and 2025, while thermal coal prices rose approximately 45% over the same period.

To improve competition, the agency proposed introducing price regulation for household and thermal coal, increasing the share of coal sold through commodity exchanges to 52%, and moving off-exchange transactions to digital trading platforms.

The report also identified several structural barriers to competition, including differences in mining contract terms and limited transparency in granting exclusive coal export rights. It further highlighted concerns over the allocation of rail capacity by the national railway operator, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy.

APDC recommended establishing transparent criteria for coal export permits, ensuring equal treatment for producers and improving disclosure of available railway capacity.

The agency also identified companies that qualify as holders of key capacity in the coal market, including Shubarkol Komir, Karazhyra, Bogatyr Komir, Kazakhmys Coal and the Eurasian Energy Corporation. Once these companies are formally recognized as holders of key capacity, they will be required to sell coal under Kazakhstan’s Rules on Equal Access to Key Capacity, which are intended to promote fair competition and equal market access.

World.title: Tokayev’s G20 Invitation Reflects Broader U.S.-Kazakhstan Strategic Momentum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan confirmed that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit in the United States (US) in December, following a meeting on Aug. 12 between Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur to discuss expanding bilateral cooperation.

Although Kazakhstan is not a member of the G20, it is among the countries invited by the US to participate in this year’s summit.

The two officials discussed preparations for the summit. They expressed readiness to coordinate on its agenda, while reviewing broader prospects for strengthening the expanded strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and the US.

Kosherbayev briefed Kapur on Kazakhstan’s ongoing political and socioeconomic reforms, describing the country as entering a new stage of development. He said the Aug. 23 Kurultai elections will represent an important milestone in implementing the country’s new constitutional model.

Kapur reaffirmed its interest in expanding practical cooperation in energy, critical minerals, advanced technologies, digitalization, transportation and investment.

Growing strategic importance

According to Assylan Smagulov, Master of Political Science and director of the Voice of Youth Public Foundation, the timing of the meeting reflects Washington’s continued strategic interest in Central Asia.

“August is traditionally a period of diplomatic coordination before a busy fall schedule of international summits. When the US holds high-level meetings with the Central Asian countries during this period, it signals that the region remains an important strategic partner. That creates additional opportunities for attracting investment and advancing national interests,” Smagulov told The Astana Times.

Smagulov noted that Kapur’s participation was particularly significant because of his expertise on South and Central Asia.

“The US sent a senior official who specializes in this region and understands both its challenges and opportunities. That demonstrates Washington views Kazakhstan as an important partner,” he said.

He added that the country’s growing geopolitical importance stems from its strategic location, transportation links and abundant natural resources, including critical minerals. These factors have become increasingly important as prolonged geopolitical tensions reshape global supply chains.

“Participation in international platforms such as the G20 creates a window of opportunities for Kazakhstan to strengthen dialogue not only with the US but also with other major powers. The broader Kazakhstan’s international engagement becomes, the greater its diplomatic flexibility and its opportunities to expand economic cooperation,” Smagulov said.

Water cooperation moves from policy to practice

Water security has also become a growing pillar of U.S.-Kazakhstan cooperation. The officials reviewed Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization as a specialized United Nations agency. The initiative aims to create a platform for coordinating international efforts on water governance, facilitating data and technology exchange and developing joint solutions to global water challenges.

The proposal entered formal international consultations during the Regional Ecological Summit held in Astana in April. A summary report from those consultations is expected to guide further negotiations among UN member states ahead of the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi later this year.

On Aug. 10, representatives of Kazakhstan’s National Hydrogeological Service (Kazgidrogeology), U.S.-based IBL Elements, and Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector met in Astana to discuss technologies for treating and reusing industrial and produced water generated during oil and gas production.

The talks focused on wastewater treatment, water reuse and the recovery of valuable and critical minerals contained in produced water. Following the meeting, Kazgidrogeology, IBL Elements and Kazakhoil Aktobe signed a trilateral memorandum of cooperation establishing a framework for pilot projects in the country’s oil and gas industry.

Rather than viewing produced water solely as industrial waste, the initiative aims to assess its potential as both a water resource and a source of strategically important minerals.

“This meeting marks an important practical step in developing cooperation between the Kazakh and American sides. The signed memorandum creates the foundation for implementing a joint pilot project and scaling successful technologies to other oil and gas facilities across Kazakhstan,” said Bolat Bekniyaz, chairman of the board of Kazgidrogeology.

Expanding economic and technology partnership

Economic ties between the two countries continue to grow. Bilateral trade exceeded $1 billion during the first half of the year, an increase of about 10% compared with the same period last year. Cumulative U.S. investment in Kazakhstan has surpassed $60 billion.

Several high-level engagements this summer underscored the growing partnership.

In June, Astana hosted the C5+1 Critical Minerals Dialogue, where senior officials from the five Central Asian countries and the United States discussed cooperation on critical mineral supply chains, investment and technology. At the event, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor described Central Asia as an increasingly important component of U.S. foreign and economic policy.

Later that month, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica Initiative and the AI Opportunity Partnership, expanding cooperation in AI, advanced technologies and high-tech manufacturing. During the Pax Silica Summit, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev signed the declaration on Kazakhstan’s accession to the initiative.

On June 30, government officials and business leaders from both countries also reaffirmed their commitment to expanding trade, investment and technological cooperation during the Kazakhstan-U.S. Business Roundtable. During the event, the two countries’ business associations signed a memorandum aimed at strengthening long-term institutional cooperation.

World.title: More than 32,000 applications for Armenian citizenship in a year: who is applying and why
World.content:
Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

“There has been a sharp increase in the number of applications for Armenian citizenship. In 2025, the number exceeded 32,000, a historic high for the entire history of the Republic of Armenia,” said Armen Kazaryan, acting deputy interior minister.

According to him, the number of citizenship applications exceeded 20,000 in each of the previous two years, compared with 7,000-8,000 in earlier years.

Kazaryan believes the main goal of applicants is to obtain a document that allows them to travel:

“We have seen certain developments, in particular the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine and restrictions on travel for Russian citizens. After that, we saw an increase in applications for Armenian citizenship. By the way, most Russian citizens applying for Armenian citizenship are ethnic Armenians.”

He rejected claims that obtaining Armenian citizenship is a complicated process:

“The requirements for ethnic Armenians are ‘zero’. People may face administrative difficulties. For example, some may lack the necessary documents proving their ethnicity, or their records may contain errors. In such cases, we need to compare the information with other records and verify it. Essentially, Armenia imposes no requirements on ethnic Armenians.”

Kazaryan himself considers the lack of requirements for ethnic Armenians problematic. In his view, this devalues the institution of citizenship itself.

“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: 'I live with the scars': Why the fight against HIV is not over
World.content:
Not long after Stephen Borg was diagnosed with HIV in 2007, he was given a warning that has remained lodged in his heart ever since.

"I was told this is a diagnosis that perhaps someone cannot love you for," Mr Borg said.

"That really sat quite heavily with me.

"If someone was diagnosed with diabetes, you might get flowers or people coming to you with open arms. That's not often the case with an HIV diagnosis."

The human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, affects the immune system and can spread through body fluids.

Left untreated, it causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

An early-detection HIV testing kit. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

As public attention has drifted toward other global health emergencies, those living with HIV, and the battle-hardened community around them, have fought tirelessly to achieve something considered internationally remarkable.

Forty-five years since the first globally diagnosed case of HIV/AIDs — and more than 40 million lives lost — Australia stands within reach of virtual elimination of HIV transmission.

But the fight is not over and the path toward that goal is not guaranteed.

The United Nations last month issued a dire warning that "the world is on course for a resurgence of the epidemic".

Experts now fear Australia's enviable position could be at risk.

"Australia is on the precipice of achieving something that to the generation before us was incomprehensible," said Dash Heath-Paynter, CEO of Health Equity Matters, the national federation for Australia's leading HIV organisations.

"It's almost like you can see the finishing line. But we can't get there with just a business-as-usual approach."

'I live with the scars'

There is a moment in the infamous 1987 Grim Reaper  where the nightmarish hooded figure crashes a black bowling ball of death into a mother, sending a baby flying from her arms.

The government-funded HIV/AIDs campaign was considered so stigmatising it was later credited with contributing to greater violence against LGBTQIA+ people.

The infamous 1987 Grim Reaper television  was taken off air halfway through its campaign. (Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive)

David Menadue was one of the first Australians diagnosed with HIV in 1984.

He watched on at the television ad with horror.

"It scared people into thinking, what am I looking at? Am I looking at a ghost or are these people like this?" Mr Menadue said.

"They became scared of people with HIV. It was very stigmatising."

David Menadue was one of the first Australians diagnosed with HIV in 1984. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter )

Fearful of the fear that surrounded them, and with no treatments available, he and a small community of people living with HIV turned to one-another for support.

"We met in each of the group's homes from 1986 to 1993, which was a bad period," he said.

"There was very good reassurance [in having] other people you could talk to."

Those meetings were essential sources of connection and comfort, but they were also places where information was shared, emerging research discussed and advocacy initiated.

The subject of death was nonetheless inescapable.

"What we didn't expect was the level of mortality," he said.

"Of the 33 people we had in that group from 86 to 93, there's only four people left.

"That's a lot of friends to die and to have to attend funerals. Each time you think, am I going to be next?

"I live with the scars even today."

David Menadue has lost many friends to HIV. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Amid the tragedy, communities like Mr Menadue's built what would become the foundation of Australia's response to HIV.

A new report from Health Equity Matters argues that "from the beginning, the Australian response was strongly community-driven" and the basis on which "a policy architecture [has] been built upon ever since".

"Community has been the most fundamental thing in my own survival," Mr Menadue said.

Change and challenge

While there remains no cure for HIV, the landscape for those with a positive diagnosis, those wanting to take preventative medication or those who simply want to get tested looks very different today.

Antiretroviral therapy has seen HIV turn from the death sentence it once was to something that, for many, can be managed as part of a long and healthy life.

The most recent data from the Kirby Institute found that of the estimated 30,000 people in Australia living with HIV, 97 per cent were receiving antiretrovirals.

Almost all of those recorded a suppressed and undetectable viral load, meaning they are at zero risk of onward transmission.

Inside an HIV testing clinic. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

The local roll-out of pre-exposure prophylaxis – known as PrEP – has equally been heralded as a "game-changer".

The HIV prevention drug was first added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) in 2018.

Sustained community advocacy has seen that access recently expanded to include non-Medicare card holders – an acknowledgement that transmission among non-citizens is just as detrimental to the Australian cause.

PrEP is now available to non-Medicare card holders. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)

"It was acknowledged that was a big gap in the response to HIV," said Chad Hughes, CEO of Thorne Harbour Health, an organisation once known as the Victorian Aids Council.

" You can't leave anybody behind in that situation. "

Public health messaging also looks very different.

Gone are the ghoulish mass campaigns, replaced by targeted and often in-place messaging.

In Perth, the state's HIV advocacy group WAAC has run health promotion campaigns, pop-up testing and PrEP prescription services on-site at a popular male sex-on-premises venue.

A free HIV testing kit on a University campus. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

There are now vending machines in every state and territory that distribute free HIV testing kits.

Positioned in discreet yet still easy-enough to find locations in university campuses and outreach settings, the vending machines have been predominantly accessed by people testing for HIV for the first time.

In Melbourne, a peer-to-peer sexual health clinic called PRONTO is staffed by people from typically non-medical backgrounds.

Peter Locke oversees the PRONTO! clinic at Thorne Harbour Health. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"What we don't want is someone to come in and behave like a clinician. We don't want [people] feeling like they're being clinically assessed," said Peter Locke, director of services for HIV clinical and community support programs at Thorne Harbour Health.

Following three months of training, employees administer free rapid finger-prick and blood tests for HIV and STIs.

The clinic's half-hour appointments – as distinct from typically shorter visits to a GP – also open the door to bigger conversations around sexual health.

Inside an HIV testing clinic. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"They may come from a religious background or a cultural background where they can't disclose [their sexual activity] to their family doctor," said Mr Locke.

"They may be married, they may be in a heterosexual relationship – they're having sex with men for a number of different reasons and they're just not going to disclose that [to a GP].

"A lot of GPs or nurses out there in the broader medical community aren't comfortable asking somebody. They'll make the assumption, 'oh, you're married, you couldn't possibly have HIV.' So they're not asking, are you having sex with men? Are you having sex with transgender people?"

Australia 'not on track' for target

Such initiatives have helped make Australia's aim of virtually eliminating HIV transmission a possibility.

The current national goal is to reach that milestone by 2030. A look to recent history suggests that may not be straightforward.

In 2014, the goal was to reach virtual elimination of transmission by 2020.

By 2020, the then Health Minister Greg Hunt updated the target to 2022.

It too was missed.

In 2023, an HIV taskforce was established with the new goal of a virtual end of transmission by 2030.

Despite the best efforts of many, and what those inside the sector call a "rare" level of multi-partisan support, new challenges are emerging that threaten to disrupt the progress.

"We're not on track," said Dr Skye McGregor, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute.

Anonymised data of HIV cases, which states and territories are required to provide to the Kirby Institute, show a consistent pattern.

Women removed as priority group for HIV reduction Women living with HIV are calling for an increase in HIV testing for women and that more funding be directed to programs in regional Australia that provide support to women with the virus.

The number of cases among Australian-born men who have sex with other men, sex workers and people who inject drugs is broadly tracking in the right direction.

It is in the roughly 30 per cent of cases involving people born overseas where more attention is needed.

"We know that the decrease [in cases] has been far higher among Australian-born people reporting male-to-male sexual contact – far closer to where we would want to be at this point," Dr McGregor said.

"But there's very different patterns in different populations.

"We're fortunate that we're at the point of needing to understand every population because we have done so well."

Chad Hughes, who has worked on HIV programs around the world for two decades, said the rise in cases among more recent arrivals to Australia can often be linked to countries with lower sexual health literacy.

Global HIV fight devastated by US funding cuts Hopes of ending the global HIV epidemic anytime soon are fading among health workers and scientists, who say new infections could increase for the first time in decades.

"A large proportion of newly diagnosed people in Australia with HIV are newly arrived people who are young, whose English is probably a second or third language, who often come as students from Southeast Asia or South America to our universities," he said.

"They come from maybe conservative backgrounds where they live with their parents, they arrive in Australia and all of a sudden they are free to go and enjoy life and go to pubs and bars and saunas and have sex and do all the things that young adults want to do without their parents watching them.

"But they don't have the knowledge and skills to protect themselves, so they're not using condoms necessarily, they're not on PrEP."

There is now a concerted push among HIV advocacy groups to better target health messaging and support services to newly arrived communities.

Marc Mendoza was diagnosed with HIV in 2018. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Marc Mendoza came to Australia from the Philippines in 1991 as a seven-year-old and grew up, by his own characterisation, "Aussie, Aussie."

He was diagnosed with HIV in 2018.

After living through "really dark days," he now volunteers as part of a support group for other people from Asian backgrounds who have tested positive.

Marc Mendoza is part of a support network for people with Asian backgrounds living with HIV. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

He said people in that community wrestle with a particular cultural stigma.

"If their families already know they're gay, it's like this other dark secret that they've now got to keep," Mr Mendoza said.

Cuts and spikes

The challenge becomes far greater beyond Australia's border.

Cuts to global public health funding, like the Trump-ordered roll backs of USAID foreign aid programs, have seen access to HIV treatments and prevention rapidly diminish.

Late last month in Rio De Janeiro, delegates at the World AIDS Conference were presented with a bleak picture.

"Never has donor funding fallen so far, so fast, and those most vulnerable are already paying the price," International Aids Society President Beatriz Grinsztejn told the conference.

An HIV awareness campaign in Fiji, where the country has been dealing with an outbreak. (ABC News: Sairusi Tabualuma)

There were 1.2 million new HIV infections in 2025, according to a UNAIDS report released at the Rio conference, of which 280,000 were recorded in Australia's neighbourhood of Asia and the Pacific.

In global terms, Australia is responsible for the merest fraction of new HIV cases – just 757 in the most recent local reporting period of 2024.

Those who work in the sector nonetheless believe the country is at a "critical time" and caution against thinking the fight against HIV is "over."

"If you get [numbers] very low and then treat it as done, it will come back with a vengeance," Mr Heath Paynter said.

"We need to be innovative and we need continued political will and investment."

David Menadue was awarded an Order of Australia Medal in the 1990s. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

David Menadue remains proud of what the decades of community activism and advocacy have achieved.

Now in his seventies, there might be a fragility to his movement, but there's a strength that refuses to leave his body.

"I think some people think because I look unwell, I must be. But my actual physical health underneath is all right," he said.

"I've got an inner strength, a resilience that all those years with HIV has probably given me.

"I'm still here."

World.title: From street to gallery, globetrotter Stormie Mill's art comes full circle
World.content:
When Stormie Mills was a teenager starting out in the world of street art, he wondered how artists got their work into the Art Gallery of WA. Forty years later, the state gallery has given him a solo exhibition.

His exhibition, All the secrets are buried between the oceans and the mountains, brings together a body of work, including two 12-metre-long paintings and a piece painted directly onto the gallery floor, which visitors will be invited to walk on.

Visitors are free to walk over the art using a mirrored surface at the gallery. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Mills, who now lives in Venice, said creating the exhibition was a beautiful way to return to his hometown.

"It's an honour and a privilege," he said.

"In my early 20s, I remember coming into the art gallery, and I remember speaking to people at the Friends of the Art Gallery in particular about how you get in here — I had no idea of how you would be exhibited.

"I was thinking like you'd bring a painting in and then hang it on the wall, so to be welcomed with such open arms and to have my ideas nurtured and to be able to do something quite so ambitious is amazing."

Stormie Mills during a street art project in Kalgoorlie. (ABC Goldfields-Esperance: Nathan Morris)

Born in the UK, Mills migrated to Perth with his family as a child, then moved back to Wales in his teens, where he first discovered street art.

Over the past 40 years, his distinctive monochrome paintings on walls and buildings have made him a well-known figure in the Perth art scene, but he said he never consciously set out to have that career.

"I've always drawn, so I'm not so sure that I had so much of an artistic career; I try to think of it as an artistic life.

"As a child, I drew; that was really what I was interested in and then in the 80s I discovered graffiti as the backdrop to a lot of movies and video clips

"There wasn't anybody to teach me any of this, so I just went out and started doing it, and it was trial and error, and it was a long way from the origins of the original New York movement, but that gave me a different sensibility.

Two Stormie Mills figures on the entrance doors to the art gallery. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

"When I did eventually go to New York, I realised that my story was very different … and I discovered that there was so much more going on in New York than just graffiti on trains.

" There was a whole genre of street art movement that had been going on for some time as well, so I just kind of married those two ideas, and I just kept travelling and kept doing stuff, and eventually it just became my whole way of life. "

When he first started painting on walls (without permission), he assumed he was being very clandestine but realised he wasn't when people began to seek him out with commissions, and he said, "it just snowballed from there".

Mills completed a number of large-scale portraits of other famous street artists on-site at AGWA for the exhibition. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

His distinctive figures in shades of grey and black aren't just an aesthetic choice; it's also a practical response to working on walls.

"When I got older, I started to think more about the process, and I decided to restrict my palette on purpose, but also the Western Australian environment was such that if you had colour in a work, it would fade really quickly.

"That drove me to think: if I want something to last, if it doesn't get painted over, the sun will bleach it, so how do I work with that?"

" I kind of worked out a process of creating this palette for myself that really worked with my sensibilities and my idea of how I wanted to try and portray emotions. "

There is unbroken continuity, by Stormie Mills, painted in 2011. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

One of the most unusual elements of the exhibition at AGWA is that a single work covers the floor in one gallery and stretches up the wall.

It also features a mirrored surface that visitors can walk on and leave their footprints.

"The whole show is about secrets and the idea of secrets and being able to reflect on your secrets, and we just thought that there would be some surface that could help facilitate that way of thinking.

"Doing things in the street — some people really care for it, and some people don't, and that the idea of people being able to walk across those works or not is entirely up to them

"I think that'll be an interesting thing to see and I think it'll cause people to pause in their process of walking through the exhibition so that'll be interesting."

Two large 12-metre paintings have been created for Stormie Mills's exhibition at AGWA. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Curator Isobel Wise said the effect, for the visitor, would be both immersive and "almost overwhelming, and she hoped the elements of the exhibition would encourage people to slow down and reflect further.

Getting Mills and his work in the gallery had come after several years of conversations.

"I'm just really excited for audiences to move through a space where they get to experience this beautiful balance of something joyous and playful that unfolds in Stormie's work," she said.

"That's also balanced with the really complex emotions that we all have as people, and his work navigates those polarities really beautifully, and it's both tender and really exciting to see how audiences are going to engage with that."

Autos (self portrait), by Stormie Mills, 2026. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The exhibition also includes an element of audience participation that could allow visitors to unburden themselves of their own secrets.

"[There is] a space next to the exhibition where people can go in and write their secrets down, and the process of writing secrets down is similar to journaling ideas," Mills said.

"When you write things down, it moves those things from one part of your brain that has no timeline to another part of your brain that does have a timeline, and that puts things in the past.

"So the idea of people being able to just let things go or unburden themselves or get rid of something will be a physical process but also helps mentally. and hopefully people will be able to go in there and get rid of some stuff."

The room, swathed in dark curtains and ambient music, will also have a shredder for people to destroy their secrets after getting them down on paper. The paper fragments will be collected by Mills and used to create an artwork at the end of the exhibition's run.

Filtered Lives, 2025, by Stormie Mills. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

In keeping with his ambition to live a creative life, a few years ago Mills and his wife Melissa moved to Venice, and his life took a fresh turn.

"I fell in love with Venice through rowing, and so I wanted to learn how to row a gondola and to row around Venice, so we moved to Venice," he said.

"I haven't got my own gondola; they're an 11-metre boat, but I'm a member of a rowing club, a couple of rowing clubs actually, and I can borrow boats, so I'm able to row around Venice."

Portrait of street artist Kid Acne, 2025-2026, by Stormie Mills. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

He hasn't stopped painting; he has been invited to be a guest of honour at the Florence Biennale next year, and he continues to paint walls.

"There's a different attitude to street art in Italy because traditionally graffiti was done by a lot of people in a lot of places," he said.

"I've been out painting at night in Italy, and people have sat and watched, and it's not seen as a bad or illegal thing; it's just somebody else making a comment about things, and it's encouraged."

All the secrets are buried between the oceans and the mountains is on display at the Art Gallery of Western Australia until November 8, 2026, and entry is free.
