World.title: The pioneering female botanical artists you may never have heard of
World.content:
Stepping into Philippa Nikulinsky's studio feels like a peek inside her mind.

From her desk overlooking the garden, to the colourful illustrations adorning the walls and drawers filled with field notes and sketches, the whole space is a culmination of a lifelong appreciation for nature.

Perth artist Philippa Nikulinsky in her home studio. (ABC Science: Peter de Kruijff)

The 83-year-old self-taught artist says her love of plants is inspired by having grown up in Kalgoorlie.

"I love the red earth country because I came from a place where it was harsh and dry and dusty, and then every few years there was an absolute miracle of wildflowers."

Vote for Australia's most amazing wildflower These 10 flowers are not just pretty faces, they have superpowers. Which one will get your vote?

Nikulinsky uses watercolour paints to create incredibly detailed and accurate depictions of Western Australia's flora.

Each artwork captures the curl and bend of leaves, the tiny segments of flowers, and branches that have become sparse over time.

She says still having a steady hand is a blessing.

In the field, she maps out her paintings on rice paper, taking notes on form and colours.

"Every drawing that I have has its own suite of field drawings".

Some of Philippa's artworks. (ABC Science: Peter de Kruijff)

Although her current paintings and illustrations focus on art rather than taxonomy, she spent decades working with scientists as a botanical illustrator.

Nikulinsky's artistic pursuits, scientific drawings and incredibly detailed field notes provide a rich record of Western Australia's floral history.

"I very seldom just do single, pretty pictures … they're actually a record of time and place."

Much like a botanist, Philippa has notebooks filled with plant specimens. (ABC Science: Peter de Kruijff)

Nikulinsky's work is part of a rich legacy of botanical illustrations created by Australian women that has made a lasting impact.

By blending art and science their illustrations inform our understanding of botany, from identifying species to providing references of landscapes that have since changed or been lost.

Scott sisters shaped the field

Harriet and Helena Scott are among the country's most influential botanical illustrators from the past.

A photo of Helena Scott and a portrait she created of her older sister Harriet on Ash Island. (Supplied: Australian Museum and State Library of NSW)

Born in 1830 and 1832 respectively, the Scott sisters were some of the earliest female commercial artists in Australia.

"That was due to their real love for the arts, for natural history [and] for the environment they were seeing around themselves," says Darcy Campbell, archivist at the Australian Museum, where an extensive collection of artworks and records from the Scott sisters are kept.

Archivist Darcy Campbell says the Australian Museum's collection includes letters written by the Scott sisters. (Supplied: Louise Reilly, courtesy of the Australian Museum)

The Sydney-born sisters developed their passion for documenting the natural world at a young age, working with their father Alexander on a shared scientific notebook.

Together they would collect specimens like moths and butterflies, building them at-home habitats and cataloguing their characteristics.

As they got older, Helena and Harriet illustrated plates for a book written by their father.

The Scott sisters were particularly interested in moths and butterflies. (Supplied: Australian Museum)

"These are beautiful artworks, quite large, very vivid in colour. And what's really interesting and unique about their work is that at the time, a lot of scientific artistic plates in scientific books would just depict the specimen … but what they were really unique for, is that they would also paint the background that they found the specimen or species in."

Despite women's contributions to science being largely unrecognised at the time, Ms Campbell says Alexander Scott insisted his daughters were credited for their work.

"He kind of is unique for his time to do that.

"So many male scientists [then] also created these kinds of books and the women in their families would be intimately involved, either by doing the illustrations or helping hand colour or helping file the papers … and the women never got credited."

Later in life, the sisters would turn to selling their artworks in order to make money. (Supplied: Australian Museum)

Ms Campbell says the legacy of the Scott sisters shines a light on both the evolution of scientific illustration and the role of women in science and art.

"It shows that women have always been involved in trying to understand the natural world.

"I think that's really true in Australia, because they also would've built on the legacies of First Nations women who had been understanding butterflies and moths for thousands of years before they ever came along."

Their legacy also carries forward today to female scientists who still use the Scott sisters' collections.

The sisters created detailed documentation of NSW's flora. (Supplied: Australian Museum)

Peggy Svoboda is one of these scientists, becoming familiar with Helena Scott's "Botany of Ash Island" in the 1990s.

The biologist was the project manager of an ecological restoration project across several sites including Ash Island, near Newcastle in New South Wales, where the Scott sisters lived from 1846.

Ms Svoboda says her team was excited to see Helena Scott's handwritten species list at the Australian Museum.

"It was just so valuable to know what that landscape had before it was modified," she says.

The 1862 document gave Ms Svoboda's team something to aim for and continues to shape revegetation efforts in the area.

Ms Svoboda also reflects on the impressive use of creative energy by the Scott sisters to document not just moths or butterflies, but the insects' whole habitat, something that is incredibly useful in restoration projects.

The incredible Margaret Flockton

Hakea bakeriana, illustrated by Margaret Flockton. (Supplied: © Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust)

Another botanical illustrator from the last century who continues to inform art and science to this day is Margaret Flockton.

She was the first scientific botanical illustrator at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Sydney.

Margaret Flockton started doing botanical illustrations in her 40s. (Supplied: © Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust)

After her family moved from the UK to Sydney in the late 1880s, Flockton worked as a lithographer, artist and then botanical illustrator.

She worked alongside the director of Royal Botanic Garden, Joseph Henry Maiden, from 1901 to 1927. During that time, she created more than 2,000 botanical illustrations.

For decades, her scientific work was largely unrecognised.

But in 2003, the Royal Botanic Garden's current illustrators, Lesley Elken and Catherine Wardrop, celebrated her story in a speech on International Women's Day.

"I think when we came across the massive collection of original artworks we had in the archive, we realised that people need to know about this amazing woman," Elken says.

Around the same time, Louise Wilson, Flockton's great great niece wrote a book about her life, called Margaret Flockton: A Fragrant Memory.

A century after her illustrations were created, Flockton's legacy inspired the creation of the Margaret Flockton Awards, which ran from 2004 to 2025.

One of Margaret Flockton's botanical illustrations of a prickly pear in Queensland. (Supplied: © Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust)

Both Elken and Wardrop have a deep appreciation for the botanical illustrators that came before them.

"You know that the drawing you're doing is always going to be there … and you want to do it justice because you know that you've got Margaret Flockton ahead of you and she was incredible, her work still blows us away," Ms Wardrop says.

Art brings science to life

Much like the botanical illustrators of previous centuries, artists continue to work with scientists to bring their observations to life.

Lesley Elken (left) and Catherine Wardrop (right) work alongside each other at the Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney. (Supplied: © Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust )

"We call we call ourselves the visual communicators of science," Ms Elken says.

Elken has worked as a botanical illustrator for three decades, sharing her role with Wardrop, who joined her just a few years later.

Alongside documenting the flora of New South Wales, a large part of their job is working with botanists to illustrate the key features of a plant, highlighting elements that make it different from its closest relative.

If you've ever used a field guide on a bush walk, it's likely you've come across these types of illustrations before.

Catherine Wardrop's illustration of Asystasia gangetica subsp. micrantha, and Lesley Elken's illustration of Genoplesium jonesii. (Supplied: © Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust)

Perhaps unsurprisingly, a common question Elken and Wardrop receive is why illustrations are used over photographs.

"Nothing compares to the capacity of an illustrator to understand the taxonomy … To work with the botanist to comprehend what the characters of the plant are," Wardrop says.

The illustrations act as a translation of scientific knowledge.

"That is a really powerful tool of scientific illustration. It speaks to everyone everywhere, not just the botanists who know how to speak the language," she says.

Illustrations document changing landscapes

Alongside documenting the minute details of a plant, Philippa Nikulinsky's artwork explores Western Australia's unique ecosystems.

"It takes me a while to sort of work out what I'm going to paint.

"I'm not looking for anything, you see… I don't look for any particular plant. It's being in the place. We stay in one spot. We don't move about… so what I paint in that place is place… And what grows with them and what lives on them, the insects, everything."

Nikulinsky's work includes two decades of illustrating covers for Landscope magazine and contributing to numerous publications and scientific articles. A book of her illustrations, Wildflowers of the Eastern Goldfields of Western Australia, was given to Queen Elizabeth II in 2011.

Nikulinsky's artworks span decades of change in the West Australian landscape. (ABC Science: Peter de Kruijff)

Nikulinsky has spent decades exploring Western Australia's diverse bushland, often alongside her husband, spending weeks camping and watching nature.

In this time, she's noticed changes in the landscape.

" I think a lot of my paintings will be all that's left, which is quite sad, but it's good that it's been done. "

Although Nikulinsky doesn't consider herself a scientist, her work continues to inspire women in scientific fields.

Perth-based botanist Keelin Smith says discovering botanical art and seeing Nikulinsky's work is one of the main reasons she decided to study botany.

"Nikulinsky's artworks are not only incredibly detailed studies of the plants themselves but how they fit into their environment," she says.

"Her work and her process for creating her work continues to inspire me to get out and see what our beautiful outback has to offer."

Some of Philippa's artworks depict a place over time. (ABC Science: Peter de Kruijff)

Nikulinsky says the comments she hears from visitors to her studio are heartwarming.

"I had a young woman come when I had open day up at the studio, and she said to me, 'I've done botany because of you.'"

"So, it gives me goosebumps, actually."

World.title: Luigi Mangione admits killing UnitedHealthcare CEO
World.content:
Luigi Mangione has admitted to fatally shooting a health insurance executive and pleaded guilty to two federal charges of stalking the executive with the intent to kill him.

The guilty plea will avert a federal trial in the closely watched case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, a brazen crime that was condemned by public officials but became emblematic of Americans' frustration with health insurance industry practices.

It could also allow Mangione, 28, to seek dismissal of state murder charges and delay an upcoming trial in that case.

US District Judge Margaret Garnett told Mangione that if he pleaded guilty, he could face a maximum sentence of life in prison on each count. Judge Garnett set Mangione's sentencing for December 18.

Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said there was no plea agreement with prosecutors.

Mr Thompson led UnitedHealth Group's insurance unit before he was shot dead in the early morning of December 4, 2024, outside the New York City hotel where an investor conference was taking place.

In court today, Mr Thompson's widow, Paulette, sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family.

Brian Thompson's widow Paulette was in court to see Luigi Mangione admit the shooting. (Reuters: David Dee Delgado)

Mangione told the court that he researched details of UnitedHealthcare's annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system.

He said he then used a 3D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Mr Thompson.

"I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione told the court.

Mr Thompson's family said in a statement that the plea marked an "important step toward justice."

"We look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family said.

No possibility of death penalty

Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social media sensation. Mangione was arrested in Pennsylvania.

He had previously pleaded not guilty in April 2025 to murder, weapons and stalking charges brought by Manhattan federal prosecutors.

Judge Garnett threw out the murder and weapons charges over legal technicalities in a surprise ruling in January 2026.

Luigi Mangione's to-do list revealed in court The documents shed new light on the steps the 27-year-old may have taken — or planned to take — to avoid capture after UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson's killing last year.

The decision eliminated the possibility that Mangione would face the death penalty in the federal case, though he still faces a possible sentence of life without parole if convicted on the remaining stalking charges.

His federal trial was most recently set for January.

Mangione separately pleaded not guilty in December 2024 to state terrorism, murder, weapons and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg.

The terrorism charges were thrown out by a judge in September 2025. A trial in that case is scheduled for September 8 before Justice Gregory Carro in Manhattan.

Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.

The guilty plea in the federal case could allow Mangione to seek dismissal of the murder charge under New York's double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct.

Mr Bragg's office would oppose the move, arguing that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges. Whoever loses would likely seek an emergency appeal.

Reuters

World.title: Hundreds evacuated from resorts as wildfires stretch across Europe
World.content:
A wildfire engulfed homes in a picturesque Croatian resort overnight, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of "very extreme" wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.

Hundreds more were evacuated from a beach resort in northern Greece and from a village in southwest France, while a major grass fire engulfed houses in England, officials said.

England's Stourbridge saw multiple homes lost after a grass fire began on the hottest day of the year. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Record-breaking heat and drought that scientists link to climate change have created ideal conditions for wildfires across Europe this summer, especially in France, Spain and Greece. The Balkans region has also endured several heatwaves.

Flames turn night sky red

Local residents and tourists described scenes of chaos as they fled in their cars from a fire outside Omis, a scenic town on Croatia's prized Dalmatian coast surrounded by trees and rocky hills.

Mario Vukucis stands next to his brother's burnt-out cafe and bar in Stanici, Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

"The flames were licking both sides of the road. When I got a little further around the bend and looked, I saw flames shooting up from under my hood. The car was on fire!" said local resident Ljubica Uglesic.

Nearly 300 fire fighters were deployed to a blaze in Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

The fire, which turned the night sky red, appeared to have calmed on Friday morning, said Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucakovic.

Authorities found one charred body while, of 40 people treated in the nearby hospital in Split, seven were in a serious condition, the hospital said.

Dinghies help in rescue from Greek seaside town

In northern Greece, people wearing face masks, some clutching children or pets, boarded dinghies and boats in the seaside town of Siviri as the fire devoured a forest and columns of smoke turned the cloudless sky a dark grey.

The coastguard said that more than 300 people had been evacuated by boat from the town, which sits on a peninsula of woodland, olive groves and beaches south of Greece's second city, Thessaloniki.

Those forced to flee found shelter through the Red Cross and tourists were among the evacuees. (Reuters: Alexandros Avramidis)

More than 140 firefighters, nine aircraft and seven helicopters were deployed to battle flames, while fishing vessels took part in the evacuation.

In Britain, Simon Markey was playing golf in Stourbridge, in central England, when he saw a fire start in a field nearby and spread quickly across the golf course despite efforts by firefighters to contain it.

It reached an area of houses, said local resident Paul Nash, whose neighbour's house burned down.

Ten homes were burnt in fires in England, while two fire fighters and a child were taken to hospital. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

"I heard a scream, and all the trees along the railway track were exploding. They weren't just setting fire, they were exploding. So we just grabbed everything and left," Mr Nash said.

In France, authorities evacuated 525 people from the village of Luglon after a wildfire broke out in the southwestern Landes region, not far from an area already devastated by major blazes this summer.

Fires near Bordeaux have remained consistent throughout summer. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Rescue services in Spain late on Thursday launched an operation to remove the remains of three kings who ruled the Aragón region in the 11th ​century from a monastery threatened by a wildfire.

An even larger fire in Huelva, in southern Spain, has burned 31,000 hectares so far and forced the evacuation of 700 people.

Only 100 kilometres from a region which saw 50,000 hectares fire-damaged last month, the south of France continues to burn. (Reuters: Stephanie Lecocq)

Firefighting planes in Spain have clocked more than 8,200 hours flying time so far this year, exceeding the number of hours flown in 2025, when a record 393,000 hectares of land burned, Spain's Environment Minister Sara Aagesen said on Bluesky.

'Very extreme' wildfire condition across Europe

The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service warned of "very extreme" conditions across a large area of central and eastern Europe, with additional pockets over southern Britain, Ireland, northern France and southern Sweden, in its outlook for the week to August 19.

By Friday a fire in Germany had affected 300 hectares of land and encroached on residential homes. (Reuters: Timm Reichert)

The average high across Western Europe on Friday was forecast to be 31.2 degrees Celsius (88 degrees Fahrenheit), which is 8 C (14 F) above what was typical from 1961 to 1990, data from the Reuters Climate Monitor showed. The temperature for Europe as a whole was 1.6 C (2.9 F) above the 1961-1990 average, it said.

The hot, dry summer is also taking a heavy toll on agriculture. Relentless heat and drought could halve this year's French maize harvest and reduce European Union production to its smallest in decades, according to analysts.

Reuters

World.title: Deborah Mailman becomes first Indigenous inductee to Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Deborah Mailman is set to become the first Indigenous person to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame.

"This means everything," Mailman, a Bidjara and Maori actor, tells ABC Radio National's Awaye!

"For me and for our mob, this isn't just recognition for me.

"It's recognition for everyone who's gone before me, who changed things for someone like me to be doing the work that I'm doing."

On Sunday Mailman will become the sixth woman to join the list in just over 40 years, following recent inductees Rebecca Gibney (2024) and Magda Szubanski (2025).

"Times are changing, thankfully, but it's 2026," Mailman says.

"To be the first [Indigenous person] — it's long overdue. Not just for me, but for anyone in this industry."

Mailman sees the milestone as a reflection of how Australian TV has changed in the last 10 to 20 years.

"Where the most exciting storytelling is coming from is the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sector," she says.

"It's just getting stronger and stronger … look at the skill that's there, that has been nurtured over a long time, to get to the point where we have so many of our mob doing incredible work."

2026 Logie nominations The annual awards show also introduced a new category honouring Australian sports journalists, named after legendary commentator Bruce McAvaney.

Mailman picked up her most recent Logie in 2024, taking out best lead actress in a drama for playing renegade politician Alex Irving in ABC TV's Total Control.

It was her sixth, following industry and publicly voted wins for shows including Mabo, Redfern Now and Mystery Road.

Speaking to ABC Arts at the Logies that year, she described how it felt to win the award for the show's final season in the year of the failed Voice to Parliament referendum.

"Over the four or so years [of making Total Control], we had a new prime minister, throw a pandemic in the middle of it, and then the country voted no," she said.

"To be part of this production that kept us [Indigenous peoples] in that focus, that kept our narrative strong, that meant everything to me. That meant everything to all of us who are part of it."

A foot in the door

Mailman's first Logie came in 2002 for her first small-screen role as the optimistic and generous Kelly Lewis in share house drama The Secret Life of Us, an award she won again in 2004.

She started her acting career on the stage, which saw her co-write and star in the seminal play The 7 Stages of Grieving in 1994, before she played Nona in director Rachel Perkins's film Radiance in 1998, landing her an AFI Award (now AACTA) for best lead actress.

Three years later she scored her breakthrough TV gig with The Secret Life of Us.

Mailman looks back fondly at making the show, which catapulted its cast, including Gold Logie winner Samuel Johnson and 2026 Logie nominee Claudia Karvan, into the mainstream.

"That experience really gave me my training in front of a camera," Mailman says.

"It introduced me to the art of filmmaking."

Mailman with her Secret Life of Us co-stars, including Claudia Karvan and Joel Edgerton. (Supplied: Network Ten)

She especially loved how relatable the storylines felt, not just to her and the rest of the cast, but to the audience.

"It was such a big new adventure for me and I just loved every moment of it," Mailman says.

There, at that apartment building in St Kilda, Mailman met lifelong friends and collaborators.

"It was my first real foot into the [screen] industry," she says.

"To be supported in the way that I have been, right from the get-go, has been really important."

Telling First Nations stories

After The Secret Life of Us, Mailman featured as Lorraine in Redfern Now (earning another Logie), as a guest star of sketch series Black Comedy, and in movies including the musicals Bran Nue Dae and The Sapphires.

In 2012 Mailman starred as Lorraine in Redfern Now. Four years later, she picked up the Logie for most outstanding actress for the telemovie. (Supplied: ABC TV)

More recently she's played Kerry in Mystery Road, Aunty Linda in Indigenous superhero series Cleverman, and a nun in Warwick Thornton's award-winning The New Boy.

Roles like these are just a handful of the Indigenous-led projects Mailman has taken on throughout her career.

"That's where a lot of my work has gravitated towards: working with my own mob and telling stories that matter to me and my family and many communities around the country," she says.

She sees it as a kind of correction after First Nations stories were excluded from Australian screens for many years.

"Our voices weren't there," Mailman says.

"Now to be part of that canon of storytelling that shows the breadth and diversity and dynamic of who we are as people and our culture and what our stories are means everything to me."

Mailman is proud to follow in the footsteps of other Indigenous trailblazers on both screen and stage, including Justine Saunders (The Fringe Dwellers), Kylie Belling (Until the End of the World) and National Black Theatre founders Bob Maza and Gary Foley.

"They were instrumental in providing opportunities that are there for me now," she says.

Mailman also admires other Indigenous community leaders and activists who are not from the performing arts world.

"They're the people I have to thank because they fought the hard fight," she says.

Mailman feels privileged to potentially inspire the next generation of First Nations actors and creatives, alongside her peers and collaborators Perkins and Leah Purcell (The Drover's Wife).

"A whole bunch of us grew up professionally together," Mailman says.

"I'm part of that community and I'm proud of that.

"I'm really proud I'm still doing what I'm doing and that I've been part of this group of artists who've led by example."

Celebrating Blak excellence

Mailman joins the Logies Hall of Fame in a year dominated by Indigenous stories and storytellers.

Half of the nominees for most popular new talent are First Nations actors: 10-year-old Eloise Hart (Mystery Road: Origin, Goolagong), Lila McGuire (Goolagong) and Tamala (Ghosts Australia).

2026 Logies: First Nations excellence With strong representation of Indigenous talent in this year's Logie nominations, actor Lila McGuire says it's a "very important time" and "a gift for young mob".

The same is true for best lead actor in a drama, with Hunter Page-Lochard (Reckless), Mark Coles Smith (Mystery Road: Origin), and Rob Collins (RFDS); and best supporting actor, with Clarence Ryan (Mystery Road: Origin) against Thomas Weatherall, nominated twice (Heartbreak High; The Narrow Road to the Deep North).

Meanwhile, Goolagong is up for best miniseries, Mystery Road: Origin for best drama program, and Miranda Tapsell's Top End Bub for best scripted comedy.

For Mailman, being recognised in the same year as so many Indigenous nominees makes being inducted into the Hall of Fame this year even more special.

"That speaks volumes to me," she says.

" It's so exciting to have that many of our actors be acknowledged in this way, which demonstrates absolutely their excellence in their craft. "

It also means being inducted in front of close friends such as Collins.

"There's going to be mob in the room!" Mailman says.

"It's going to be a real joy to have that energy, to know that everyone else is being celebrated along with me.

"It's just a big warm hug."

World.title: Multi-million dollar art recovered after three-minute Italian museum heist
World.content:
Three century-old paintings believed to have been stolen by an organised gang have been recovered, months after the criminals broke into an Italian museum in a three-minute heist.

The fine artworks are the 1919 impressionist painting Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's 1887 Still Life with Cherries, and the 1922 Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Authorities said the Cézanne was valued at six million euros ($9.79 million), the Renoir at three million euros ($4.89 million), and the Matisse at 20,000 euros ($32,665).

Fish by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Italy's Carabinieri, the domestic police force, and its cultural heritage protection unit confirmed in a statement on Friday, local time, the paintings were discovered during searched ordered by prosecutors.

The police did not provide details of the searches, but said investigations into the heist were ongoing.

Cup And Plate Of Cherries by Paul Cezanne. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

How Italy's three-minute art museum heist unfolded

The heist at the Italy's Magnani Rocca Foundation, located about 20 kilometres south of Parma in the country's north, took place on the night of March 22, according to police.

Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Authorities at the time said they believed the masked thieves forced open an entrance door, while local media reported they managed to take the paintings in less than three minutes before escaping across the museum's gardens.

In the days after the heist, Italy's La Repubblica newspaper reported the thieves entered the museum's grounds via an unlit, country access road after sawing three bars off a back gate.

They then forced the building's front door open with a crowbar and accessed the museum's French Room on the upper floor by breaking down its doors, the outlet said.

CCTV from inside the museum shows the masked thieves removing the works of art from the walls of an upper floor room. (Reuters: Supplied/Carabineiri Parma)

The newspaper said an interior alarm startled the group, who then fled and were believed to have lost a fourth painting — the three million euro ($4.9 million) Paysage de Cagnes also by Renoir — during their escape.

Carabinieri officers and private security contractors who arrived at the museum later said they spotted the group on thermal imaging cameras while inside the building, but were unable to stop them fleeing.

The Magnani Rocca Foundation was established by art historian Luigi Mangini in 1977, aimed at promoting cultural activities around art, music and literature.

The security vision also shows the thieves running through an open foyer area to escape through a window. (Supplied: Carabineiri Parma)

The foundation hosts Mr Mangini's collection of art and also includes works by Dürer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.

Apart from its showcased art, the building is known for its spacious gardens, often roamed by a muster of white peacocks.

Mr Mangini lived in the greenhouse on the villa's grounds until his death in 1984.

Experts stunned by theft of 'recognisable' art

During its investigation of the heist, the Carabinieri's RIS forensic agency and the force's dedicated art recovery squad analysed CCTV footage from the villa on the night of the theft.

Magnani Rocca Foundation museum villa is renowned for its spacious gardens and white peacocks. (Instagram: Francesca Fietta/magnanirocca)

La Repubblica reported in April that authorities believed the gang consisted of up to five people, who police were trying to "height match" as part of identikit efforts.

One source told Reuters they had been surprised at the thieves' choice of works of relatively low value from the museum's permanent collections.

The ⁠lack of commercial insurance in Italy for paintings like those that were stolen is not uncommon, market sources say.

Art historian Silvia Evangelisti told La Repubblica the heist was "a very strange theft".

"These works are so recognisable that it's impossible to imagine the market they could be sold on," she said.

"They could have stolen older works, which Luigi Magnani's precious and refined collection is full of.

"Perhaps they were disturbed by their location on the first floor; they were in a hurry to act so they could escape more quickly."

Italian art expert Claudio Strinati echoed that sentiment.

"Renoir's painting — for example — is very beautiful but, within the context of the foundation as a whole, it isn't among the most important works," he told The Associated Press.

Simone dall'Orto, the mayor of the Traversetolo commune to the south-east of the museum, said the thievery had "dismayed" local residents.

"It affects not only an artistic heritage of extraordinary value, but the very identity of our community," he said.

The crime also followed a series of high-profile heists at major European museums, including the stunning theft in October of French crown jewels and other items worth 88 million euros ($143.7 million) from the Louvre in Paris.

ABC/Wires

World.title: ‘Swung wildly’: Second UK train derails in as many days amid heatwave
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeTrains ‘Swung wildly’: Second UK train derails in as many days amid heatwave David Crowe August 15, 2026 — 4:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A second train has derailed near London one day after a similar accident on major railway lines near the British capital, amid soaring heat and concerns about safety. Two carriages on the train from Southend to London left the tracks as the train came to a halt in a plume of dust and smoke, with witnesses reporting a crash that shook nearby shops. Two carriages on the train from Southend to London left the tracks near Wickford in Essex. BBC Ambulance officials said all 62 passengers were taken from the train safely at the town of Wickford, east of London, with no casualties among those on board. The accident followed the derailment of a similar train at Lewes on a journey from London to Eastbourne, south of the capital, the previous day. This left two passengers seriously injured, and nine others also injured.



The two incidents are yet to be investigated, and officials cautioned against speculating about their causes, although one engineering expert has said welded rails might buckle if they were unable to expand in the heat. Temperatures soared to 38 degrees in London on Thursday, the day of the first accident, and reached 34 degrees on Friday, when the second train derailed. Passengers on the first train reported it “sliding” across the tracks before some of the carriages left the line, tipped over and ended in a field alongside the line. Photographs from the accident showed passengers standing in carriages that had rolled on their side. Members of the Rail Accident Investigations Bureau (RAIB) on the tracks at the scene where a train derailed near Lewes railway station in East Sussex. James Manning/PA via AP The second train, operated by Greater Anglia with 10 carriages, came to a halt shortly after 2pm on Friday afternoon (soon after 11pm on Friday, AEST). The carriages remained upright.



One passenger told the BBC that everybody on the train appeared to be safe. “The train swung wildly for around 10 seconds, like it was about to tilt over,” said Jon Young, 37. “It then carried on going for a couple of minutes, but there was a horrible vibrating sound, so something obviously wasn’t right. “Then the train came to a halt and there was smoke coming from the back carriage.” Photographs from the scene showed two helicopters landing near the train, apparently ready to rush passengers to hospital if necessary.



The East England Ambulance Service said it dispatched a significant number of resources, including its hazardous response team and critical care specialists from charity partners. “Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train. Following assessment, all patients were discharged at scene,” it said. “We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment. There were no casualties among those on board.” Network Rail, the public agency responsible for the railway lines, said it was investigating both incidents.



The agency’s group safety and engineering director, Martin Frobisher, said he appreciated the concern about two derailments over two days, but said the British network was among the safest in the world. Related Article Updated

Trains ‘We just went over’: Passenger train from London derails, flips “The Rail Accident Investigation Branch is conducting an investigation into the derailment at Lewes, and has investigators on scene at the Wickford incident,” he said. “We would ask people to avoid speculating on the cause of any incidents until further information is available. “The unprecedented hot and dry weather that we have experienced this summer has presented exceptional challenges to the railway.



“In response, we have taken several additional proactive steps to manage and mitigate the impact on the railway, including closely monitoring the temperature of tracks, implementing speed restrictions where it is appropriate to do so, and planning track renewals around high temperatures.” Some experts suggested the heat could have played a role in the accident at Lewes. William Powrie, a professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton, told London’s Telegraph that continuously welded rails could buckle if they were unable to expand in hot weather, and the hard, dry ground could also cause track deformities “Therefore, this incident could be hot weather related, but the exact causal chain of events needs to be established through proper and thorough investigation,” Powrie said. World.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in federal case, admits killing insurance CEO
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in federal case, admits killing insurance CEO Jack Queen August 15, 2026 — 2:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luigi Mangione has admitted in court to fatally shooting a health insurance executive and pleaded guilty to two federal charges of stalking the executive with the intent to kill him. The guilty plea will avert a federal trial in the closely watched case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, a brazen crime that was condemned by public officials but became emblematic of Americans’ frustration with health insurance industry practices. A courtroom sketch depicts Luigi Mangione sitting between his attorneys on August 14. AP It could also allow him to seek dismissal of state murder charges and delay an upcoming trial in that case. US District Judge Margaret Garnett told Mangione that if he pleaded guilty, he could face a maximum sentence of life in prison on each count. Garnett set Mangione’s sentencing for December 18.



Mangione’s lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said there was no plea agreement with prosecutors. Thompson led UnitedHealth Group’s insurance unit before he was shot dead in the early morning of December 4, 2024, outside the hotel where an investor conference was taking place. Thompson’s widow sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family. Mangione, 28, said in court that he researched details of UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system. He said he then used a 3-D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Thompson. “I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said. Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York on August 11. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP



Graphic footage of the killing and a five-day manhunt for a suspect made the case a media fixture and social media sensation. Mangione was arrested in Pennsylvania. He had previously pleaded not guilty in April 2025 to murder, weapons and stalking charges brought by Manhattan federal prosecutors. Garnett threw out the murder and weapons charges over legal technicalities in a surprise ruling in January 2026. The decision eliminated the possibility that Mangione would face the death penalty in the federal case, though he still faces a possible sentence of life without parole if convicted on the remaining stalking charges. Related Article Crime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? His federal trial was most recently set for January. Mangione separately pleaded not guilty in December 2024 to state terrorism, murder, weapons and forgery charges brought by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. The terrorism charges were thrown out by a judge in September 2025. A trial in that case is scheduled for September 8 before Justice Gregory Carro in Manhattan. Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.



The guilty plea in the federal case could allow Mangione to seek dismissal of the murder charge under New York’s double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct. Bragg’s office would oppose the move, arguing that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges. Whoever loses would likely seek an emergency appeal. World.title: I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip
World.content:
★★★ CultureTV & radioStreaming I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip Jared Richards August 15, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lanterns ★★★ Superheroes and mortals alike return to the same question in HBO Max’s gritty, psychological take on DC’s Green Lantern franchise: “Are you afraid?” The three words become a mantra for John Stewart (Aaron Pierre, Rebel Ridge; The Morning Show), a Lantern-in-training assigned to follow around Earth’s long-standing Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler, Friday Night Lights). Together, they investigate a strange shooting in Nevada with suspected intergalactic links. Kyle Chandler as Green Lantern Hal Jordan in Lanterns. Warner Bros Without mental resolve, these intergalactic law officers can’t use their weapons – a magical emerald green ring that lets them fly and create objects, force fields and more out of sheer mind power. But fear itself is the powering force of Lanterns, a show that examines how it is used to justify acts of love, war and hatred across interpersonal relationships and intergalactic colonialism alike.



Created by Chris Mundy (Ozark) and produced by Damon Lindelof (Watchmen; The Leftovers) and DC writer Tom King, Lanterns is a detective drama first and a superhero show second, though there’s a solid amount of cheesy jokes and quips. Don’t worry: that dark, moody edge isn’t an excuse for terrible lighting or filters. Lanterns offers crisp visuals. Editor's pick ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage At first, John and Hal couldn’t seem more opposite. While Hal’s decades of power and fame has left him arrogant and smarmy, John is comparatively robotic, a stoic ex-military man emotionally cauterised by a traumatic childhood. In Lantern’s opening scene, he barely reacts when his father draws a close-range rifle in their backyard for a William Tell trick, shooting an apple atop his head. Both men are fearless, but through flashbacks across the seven of eight episodes offered for review, it’s revealed that their mental fortitude is not equal. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lantern’s most intriguing, understated qualities.



With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a local sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. Lanterns streams on HBO Max from August 17.

World.title: Deborah Mailman makes history as first Indigenous person inducted into Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.

The terrorism charges were thrown out by a judge in September 2025. A trial in that case is scheduled for September 8 before Justice Gregory Carro in Manhattan. Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.



The guilty plea in the federal case could allow Mangione to seek dismissal of the murder charge under New York’s double jeopardy law, which protects people from being prosecuted twice for the same conduct. Bragg’s office would oppose the move, arguing that the murder charge is legally distinct from the federal charges. Whoever loses would likely seek an emergency appeal. World.title: I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip
World.content:
★★★ CultureTV & radioStreaming I’m not really into traumatic superhero stories, but Lanterns had me in its grip Jared Richards August 15, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lanterns ★★★ Superheroes and mortals alike return to the same question in HBO Max’s gritty, psychological take on DC’s Green Lantern franchise: “Are you afraid?” The three words become a mantra for John Stewart (Aaron Pierre, Rebel Ridge; The Morning Show), a Lantern-in-training assigned to follow around Earth’s long-standing Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler, Friday Night Lights). Together, they investigate a strange shooting in Nevada with suspected intergalactic links. Kyle Chandler as Green Lantern Hal Jordan in Lanterns. Warner Bros Without mental resolve, these intergalactic law officers can’t use their weapons – a magical emerald green ring that lets them fly and create objects, force fields and more out of sheer mind power. But fear itself is the powering force of Lanterns, a show that examines how it is used to justify acts of love, war and hatred across interpersonal relationships and intergalactic colonialism alike.



Created by Chris Mundy (Ozark) and produced by Damon Lindelof (Watchmen; The Leftovers) and DC writer Tom King, Lanterns is a detective drama first and a superhero show second, though there’s a solid amount of cheesy jokes and quips. Don’t worry: that dark, moody edge isn’t an excuse for terrible lighting or filters. Lanterns offers crisp visuals. Editor's pick ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage At first, John and Hal couldn’t seem more opposite. While Hal’s decades of power and fame has left him arrogant and smarmy, John is comparatively robotic, a stoic ex-military man emotionally cauterised by a traumatic childhood. In Lantern’s opening scene, he barely reacts when his father draws a close-range rifle in their backyard for a William Tell trick, shooting an apple atop his head. Both men are fearless, but through flashbacks across the seven of eight episodes offered for review, it’s revealed that their mental fortitude is not equal. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lantern’s most intriguing, understated qualities.



With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a local sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. Lanterns streams on HBO Max from August 17.

World.title: Deborah Mailman makes history as first Indigenous person inducted into Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.
